bio.en: Sam Lessin is a partner at Slow Ventures, former VP of Product at Facebook, and a two-time founder, who joined Lenny to talk about the surprisingly high-leverage skill of proper etiquette.
bio.zh: Sam Lessin 是 Slow Ventures 的合伙人、Facebook 前产品副总裁、两次创业者，他做客本期，聊的是一个出人意料却极具杠杆效应的技能：得体的社交礼仪。

summary.en: Sam makes the case that etiquette is a practical skill for showing up in a room with a low heart rate - earning trust and influence without unnecessary friction. He walks through rules for introductions, being early, eye contact, handling late arrivals, and introducing partners, drawn from his book and classes. The episode is an unconventional but genuinely useful guide to the soft skills that quietly shape careers.

You're not just a potential check for whatever it's going to be. So there's a bunch of things like that. I'm kind of curious. We can go through a bunch more, but those are some of the ones I would think about.
turns.zh: 对。早到。这是第一条。再说一遍，我这么说，是作为一个坦白的人——我活在自己的 hypocrisy 里。我经常不早到，但你该早到。你不需要早到半小时，那有点怪，但确保你留点缓冲时间，这样——再说一次，想想低心率。如果你气喘吁吁提前五分钟冲进房间，你的心率是高的。（00:10:37）：如果你进来，在等候室里停一下缓口气。是他们让你等的。这是我想要培养的动态。现在，如果你没早到——抱歉，如果你不是早到而是迟到了——就道个歉。不需要搞得像 511 那样，再说一次，这又回到心率那个点上。你可以简单道个歉，然后继续。我见过太多次人们把这件事搞砸：慌慌张张、手忙脚乱地进来，你心里想：『没事，我们理解。』（00:11:02）：所以我觉得这是另一个挺明显、但也挺重要的点。我还见过、也常聊到的另一些是：你要有一个有力的握手，坚定，但别把人家手捏碎。再说一次，这不是拿你朋友练的。还有，重复对方的名字，是件非常、非常有价值的、值得琢磨的事。当你见到一个人，说：『嘿 Lenny，很高兴认识你。』为什么？因为它表明你真的在努力记住对方的名字。（00:11:31）：很多时候人会见很多人。如果只是很高兴认识你然后就走开，首先，你会更难记住对方的名字。其次，它其实表明你见到、并努力去建立连接、说『好，我在努力聚焦你。你对我不是个数字。』你对我也不是一张潜在的支票什么的。所以类似这样的事有一堆。我有点好奇，我们可以再过一堆，但那些是我会先想的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One that I loved was if somebody else is late, do not make them feel bad and do the opposite of what you're doing, of what you do.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢的一条是：如果别人迟到了，别让人难堪，而且要反其道而行——别学你自己的做法。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: 100%. And I think this is like, I've seen this with entrepreneurs. And I get I'm a VC. I do get scheduled in 30 minute chunks back to back all the time, especially on Zoom. Guess what? I am frequently late. I don't feel good about it, but it happens. And a lot of times, founders, most of the time I'd say founders know that if I'm late, I will always apologize. I'll try to email them ahead, et cetera, but then it is what it is and we kind of get right into it. (00:12:26): Every once in a while, you'll have some founder who is super indignant about it. It's fine if you feel that way, but it's really not very productive to make a big deal out of it. If this is a deal breaker for you that I was a few minutes late, then now I feel like I'm wasting the next 25 minutes of my meeting time because this is going to be the wrong dynamic, and so I just think there's like, don't harp on it. It's okay.
turns.zh: 百分之百。我觉得这就像……我在创业者身上见过。我懂，我是风投，我整天都被排成 30 分钟一格、一格接一格的会，尤其 Zoom 上。你猜怎么着？我常常迟到。我对此感觉不好，但它就是会发生。很多时候，创始人——我想说大多数时候——知道如果我迟到，我一定会道歉。我会尽量提前发邮件告诉他们等等，但既然发生了，我们就直接进入正题。（00:12:26）：偶尔，你会遇到某个创始人，对此超级愤慨。如果你这么想那也行，但搞得好像天塌了一样真的没什么建设性。如果我迟到几分钟对你来说是 deal breaker，那我现在就觉得，接下来的 25 分钟我都在浪费，因为这会变成错误的动态。所以我觉得就是——别纠结，没事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and also some advice on eye contact. Share that one.
turns.zh: 对，还有关于眼神交流的建议。分享一下那条。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's really important. Again, I think the thing I keep in mind is especially in an age where everyone's used to being in front of computer screens and looking at six different windows at the same time. Again, people are taking their time to meet with you or at a party, they're taking their time to listen to you. And it's just a matter of respect to be like, "I'm actually here in this conversation. I'm not off on my screen. I'm not glancing around the room." (00:13:17): Now look, there are some people, we all know this who are literally quite neurodivergent and that's very hard for them. That happens, and a lot of founders have neurodivergence in some ways. So there is grace in this to a point, but it's a thing you should make at least an effort. I think one of the most important things about all this stuff is what matters in some ways is the signaling of the effort as much as the actual thing. I think it's a really big overarching theory. So it's like, "Look, if you have trouble with this, but you're really trying, that goes a long way." Versus just being like, whatever.
turns.zh: 这真的很重要。再说一次，我觉得要记住的关键是，尤其在这个人人都习惯对着电脑屏幕、同时看六个不同窗口的时代。再看一次，人家是抽出时间来见你，或者在派对上，他们抽出时间来听你说话。『我真的在这个对话里，我没在看我的屏幕，我没在扫视房间』——这只是一个尊重的问题。（00:13:17）：现在看，有些人——我们都知道——确实是神经多样性的，对他们来说这很难。那会发生，而且很多创始人在某些方面就是神经多样性的。所以这里面有一定的 grace，到某个程度。但它是一件你至少该努力的事。我觉得所有这些事里最重要的一点之一是：在某种程度上，你付出努力这个信号，和事情本身一样重要。我觉得这是一个很大的 overarching 理论。所以就像：『看，如果你在这方面有困难，但你真的在努力，那会很有用。』而不是一副随便啦的样子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe a final tip there is around partners, introducing the partner, saying hi to their partner, share that one.
turns.zh: 也许最后一条建议是关于伴侣的——介绍伴侣、跟伴侣打招呼，分享一下那条。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah. So look, this happens all the time. And again, in the spirit of, I'm not permitted at this either, if you're with your partner, introduce them first. Bring them into the conversation. One great trick we talk about in the book, which I really unfortunately use all the time is there's this whole thing. Let's pretend you're with your partner or with someone who's a friend. It doesn't have to be romantic partner, whoever you're with. You're going to forget someone's name, and what you really should do is-
turns.zh: 对。看，这种事一直在发生。再说一次，本着我在这件事上也不达标的精神：如果你和伴侣在一起，先介绍他们。把他们带进对话里。书里我们聊到的一个很棒、说实话我老在用的小技巧是：有整个一套做法。假设你和伴侣，或者和一个朋友在一起。不一定是恋爱伴侣，是谁都行。你会忘掉某人的名字，而你真正该做的是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All the time. All the time.
turns.zh: 一直这样。一直这样。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: You get the friend's name and that's what you're supposed to do. The etiquette is you say, "Lenny, please meet my wife, Jessica." And that kind of thing. Now here's the thing, this is where you start betting rules. What if I don't remember your name? If you have your partner with you, you can flip it around and say, "Jessica, I want to introduce you." And then you can kind of figure out how to frame it up so that you then Lenny extends your hand and say, "It's really nice to meet you, Jessica." And you get to pick up the name again or things like that. So there are some-
turns.zh: ——你该先说出朋友的名字，那是你该做的。礼仪的做法是你说：『Lenny，请认识一下我太太 Jessica。』诸如此类。但现在的问题是，这就是你开始打规则擦边球的地方。如果我不记得你的名字怎么办？如果你带着伴侣，你可以反过来说：『Jessica，我想介绍你。』然后你就能想办法把它框定好，让 Lenny 伸出手说：『很高兴认识你，Jessica。』你于是又能捡回那个名字，之类的。所以有一些——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You let it hang, that's the craziest-
turns.zh: 你让它悬在那里，那是最疯的——

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: ... which by the way-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's a great example of the fact that if you're really in tune socially, you kind of know what's going on. You know what I mean? You're not an idiot. You know, "Oh, what is proper? What this person is doing?" There's a gap between it. There's a reason. The reason is, but it's at least enough plausible deniability of semi-bad etiquette that leverages the social situation to be a better etiquette, that it's a useful thing to think about as a small queue.
turns.zh: 这是个很好的例子，说明如果你在社交上真的很敏锐，你其实知道发生了什么。你懂我意思吧？你不是白痴。你会想：『哦，什么是得体的？这个人在做什么？』这中间有个 gap。是有原因的。原因就是，但至少它给了你足够的合情合理的推诿空间——用这个社交情境来变成更好的礼仪——把它当成一个小的 cue 去思考，是有用的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm so bad at remembering names. I think I have a medical issue, so I just can't remember names. So this tip alone is so good. And just to reinforce it, so there's almost two ways to do this is what you're describing. Either it's like my wife's name's Michelle, so it's like, "Hey, Michelle. I meet my wife, Michelle." And then they're like, "Oh, I'm Bob. Nice to meet you, Michelle." Or make it a little more awkward of just, "Michelle, meet and then let it hang." Is that the thing?
turns.zh: 我特别不擅长记名字。我觉得我有医学问题，就是记不住名字。所以光这一条就太好了。再强调一下，你说的做法几乎有两种。要么就像：我太太叫 Michelle，所以是『嘿，Michelle。我介绍我太太 Michelle。』然后对方说：『哦，我是 Bob。很高兴认识你，Michelle。』或者搞得稍微尴尬一点：『Michelle，来认识一下——』然后让它悬在那儿。是那样吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: "Michelle, I want to introduce you." Or something like that.
turns.zh: 『Michelle，我想介绍你。』或者类似的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to introduce you. Okay.
turns.zh: 我想介绍你。好。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Something like that, or I want to introduce you to Michelle. You look at them in the eye, and then your wife would be like, "Hi, I'm Michelle. Remind me your name or it's nice to meet you." Or whatever it ends up being. Look, I also, for what it's worth, I actually have such a clinical problem on name face recognition that actually runs in our family. I have this whole backstory, which is part ... and I worked at Facebook for a long time, was really into it early on. (00:16:06): No kidding. I think part of my early attraction to the platform was it was the first time you walk around college and you're like, "I know these people, I just don't remember their names." You're like, "Oh my God, there's a resource I can study." And this was a very valuable social thing for me. So I'm with you. I have the same problem I think a lot of people do.
turns.zh: 类似这样的话，或者我想把你介绍给 Michelle。你看着他们的眼睛，然后你太太就会说：『嗨，我是 Michelle。提醒我一下你的名字，或者很高兴认识你。』或者最终变成别的什么。看，顺便说，其实我自己在名字-脸识别上也有这么个临床级别的问题，而且这在我们家是遗传的。我有一整个背景故事，是其中的一部分……我在 Facebook 工作了很久，早期就特别着迷于它。（00:16:06）：不骗你。我想我早期被这个平台吸引的部分原因就是：那是你第一次在大学校园里走来走去，心想我认识这些人，只是记不住他们名字。你心想：『哦天哪，有个我可以研究的资源了。』这对我来说是非常有价值的社交工具。所以我挺你。我有同样的问题，我想很多人都有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's move on to conversations. Give us some tips.
turns.zh: 好。我们进到对话部分。给我们一些建议。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: So I mean, on the conversation front, I think the key again is to welcome people into the conversation. Consider it, especially you see this happen sometimes, especially when there's weird power dynamics at play. You'll see some famous VC or founder walk into the room, and then some young startup person will waylay them and almost flock them off and they're really excited to talk to this person, but you're like, there's a bunch of people around and the more you can be inclusive and low heart rate, it's not a scarcity mindset, it's an abundance mindset. (00:16:58): I think that's kind of the tone to think about in terms of what a conversation is and how to show up in a room and meet with people. Another really big one we harp on a lot in the book in a bunch of the panels is ask questions, but there's a limit. So asking questions is great. (00:17:16): You're coming in and says, "Hey, it's nice to meet you. Let me give you my four-minute startup spiel and everything I'm into da-da-da." So self-centered. It kind of misses the point that a conversation is a give and a get and it should be an exchange. And so when you go in with a mindset of I should ask questions, that's great. (00:17:32): There is doing it too much, which is when it's done in a forced way, sometimes I feel this, you'll meet someone and you feel like it's the inquisition or all they're trying to do is extract information to you and giving you nothing in return. This happens sometimes. And so I think, again, this is about balance, this is about low heart rate. I do think questions are a great tool to engage someone, but don't make it six questions in a row and make sure there's always in some ways a give to get. (00:18:00): If you can come in, the best conversations are coming, someone comes in and gives you an idea or has a point or sparks something, then it's like a game of ping pong, then you can kind of react to and it goes back and forth where there's openness and they're playing with you, not playing single player is almost the way I would think about it in a conversation.
turns.zh: 在对话这块，我觉得关键再次是 welcoming people into the conversation。尤其你有时能看到，尤其当存在奇怪的权力动态时。你会看到某个有名的风投或创始人走进房间，然后某个年轻的创业者会拦住他们、几乎把他们劫走，他们真的很兴奋能跟这个人说话，但你心里想：周围还有一堆人呢，你越能做到包容、低心率——这不是稀缺心态，是丰盈心态。（00:16:58）：我觉得这就是关于什么是对话、如何出现在房间里与人相处该有的基调。我们在书里、在好多场座谈里反复强调的另一条大原则是：问问题，但要有个限度。所以问问题很好。（00:17:16）：你进来就说：『嘿，很高兴认识你。让我给你来一段四分钟的创业 pitch，以及我所有感兴趣的东西，吧啦吧啦。』太以自我为中心了。它错过了重点：对话是一种给予也是获取，应该是有来有往的交换。所以当你带着我该问问题的心态进来，那很好。（00:17:32）：但做过头就成了——当你做得太刻意，有时我会有这种感觉：你遇到一个人，觉得像是在受审讯，或者他们只想从你这儿榨取信息、什么都不回馈。这有时会发生。所以我觉得，再说一次，这是关于平衡，关于低心率。我确实认为问问题是吸引一个人的好工具，但别连问六个问题，而且一定要确保总有某种给予来对应获取。（00:18:00）：最好的对话是：有人进来，给你一个想法、抛出一个观点、点燃了什么，然后就像打乒乓球，你回应、它再打回来，一来一回，彼此开放、在和你玩……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the tip here. So it's basically indexed towards asking questions, but not 100% you asking questions?
turns.zh: 所以这里的建议是，大体上偏向问问题，但不是 100% 都你问？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, consider almost, put it this way, imagine you're playing ping pong or tennis or whatever you want. Hit the ball back, right? That's the question and they'll hit it back to you and then you hit it back to them. That's kind of what the flow should be. If you hit 10 balls at them in a row, you know what I mean? Or that's kind of not the vibe you want to go for.
turns.zh: 对，差不多可以这样说——换个说法，想象你在打乒乓球或网球，随便什么。把球打回去，对吧？那就是问题，他们会打回给你，然后你再打回去给他们。这差不多就是该有的节奏。如果你连着朝他们砸十个球，你懂我意思吧？或者那样就不是你想要的 vibe 了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep. Awesome.
turns.zh: 对。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Look, we talk a lot about matching vocabulary. You're going to meet a lot of different people. You want to make people feel good and welcome. I'm not saying that you should walk into a room and start talking and jibe, but I am saying if you're speaking to a university professor versus a 12-year-old, if they're using a certain level of vocabulary words, again, the point is to meet people where they're at in a way that makes them feel relaxed and good, not try to mirror them, if that makes sense. But there is a subtlety that I think really matters to it.
turns.zh: 看，我们聊了很多匹配词汇。你会遇到很多不同的人。你想让人感觉良好、被接纳。我不是说你该走进房间就开始胡言乱语般地套近乎，但我的意思是，如果你在跟一位大学教授说话，对比跟一个 12 岁小孩，如果他们用的是某种词汇水平，再说一次，重点是在他们所在的位置上跟他们相遇，让他们感到放松、舒服，而不是去模仿他们——如果这说得通的话。但这里有个微妙的差别，我觉得真的很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. There's a few more I'll point out real quick. Connecting to this idea of asking questions, not trying to give your whole spiel constantly, this idea of leaving them wanting more.
turns.zh: 酷。还有几个我快速提一下。接着问问题这个想法、别一直不停地讲你自己的那一整套——就是留点余味让人想更多这个点。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yes. This is important. I think in the end of the day, most interactions, let's put it you meet someone you're really interested in or whatever. If we're being transactional about it, what's the real goal? The real goal is to leave people in a position where they're like, "Wow, that was a really interesting person. I'd love to hear from them again or meet with them again." Or maybe even better, every once in a while this will happen. (00:19:45): It's like, "Wow, that's a really interesting person or idea." The person walks across the room someone else is like, "Hey, you really should talk to Lenny. Shout to Sam." You want to leave them being like, "That's interesting and I like to continue this or expand it." Not, "I just heard this entire person's life story, I never need to talk to them again." And so I do think there's, again, leave them wanting more, I think is important. And that is partially about knowing when to excuse yourself gracefully as much as it is about when to enter.
turns.zh: 对。这很重要。我觉得说到底，大多数互动——这么说吧，你遇到一个你真的很感兴趣的人，之类的。如果我们功利地看，真正目标是什么？真正目标是让人处在一个状态：『哇，那是个真有意思的人。我想再听到他的消息，或者再和他见一面。』或者也许更好——偶尔会发生这种事。（00:19:45）：就像：『哇，那是个真有意思的人，或者有个真有意思的想法。』那个人穿过房间，另一个人就说：『嘿，你真该去和 Lenny 聊聊。代我向 Sam 问好。』你想让人留下的是：『这有意思，我想继续下去或者展开。』而不是我刚听完了这人整整一生的故事，我再也不需要跟他说话了。所以我觉得，再说一次，留点余味让人想更多，很重要。而这在一定程度上，是关于懂得何时优雅地告退，和懂得何时进入一样重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And again, this comes back to this idea of abundance. This isn't your one shot. You'll have other opportunities. People don't want to feel like you're just on them just trying to-
turns.zh: 再说一次，这又回到丰盈这个想法。这不是你唯一的机会。你还会有机遇。人们不想感觉你只是在缠着他们、想——

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I've had this conversation with so many, and I think it's a uniquely American and honestly a uniquely Silicon Valley thing. I'll go so far to say that, which is, look, we're used to, especially if you're young and these are big opportunities or big moments, people are kind of used to this environment of scarcity. It reminds me of the Eminem song when he talks about, I have one shot, one opportunity.
turns.zh: 我和太多人聊过这个，我觉得这是一种独特的美国式、坦白讲也是独特的硅谷式的东西。我甚至想说，看，我们习惯了——尤其当你年轻、这些都是大机会或大时刻——人们习惯这种稀缺的环境。这让我想起 Eminem 那首歌，他唱到：我只有一次机会，一个机遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's ... Oh, Eminem. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 我觉得是……哦，Eminem。对对对。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's a great song. It's a great song. It's great beat. Every once in a while before a big presentation, you got to listen to it and pump yourself up. But actually, again, in terms of putting people at ease and building relationships and etiquette, even if in your heart of hearts, you're like, "This really is my one shot." (00:21:00): You kind of want to show up with the self-confidence and the calm of abundance, being like, "This is not going to be my only opportunity. This is an opportunity. I'm excited to be here. I'm engaged. This is part of the story. This is not the entire story." And I think if you kind of remind yourself of that, you remind yourself that it's okay to not know everything, you keep focusing on low heart rate, engagement, eye contact, you get so much of the way there.
turns.zh: 那是首好歌。好歌。节奏好。偶尔在重要演示前，你得听它来给自己打气。但实际上，再说一次，就让人放松、建立关系和礼仪而言，哪怕你心底里觉得这真是我的唯一机会，（00:21:00）：你多少还是该带着丰盈的自信和冷静登场，像在说：『这不是我唯一的机会。这是个机会。我在这里很兴奋。我投入其中。这是故事的一部分，不是全部。』我觉得如果你这样提醒自己，提醒自己不知道一切也没关系，你持续聚焦在低心率、投入、眼神交流上，你就已经走完大半路程了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also have a tip about how to handle famous people that you might meet.
turns.zh: 你还有一条关于如何应对你可能遇到的名人的建议。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: There's so many ways. There's a bunch of tips about, I think, generally famous people, but I think there's this thing which is not being sycophantic is what I basically say, but also not being ridiculous is almost the way I would frame it in this conversation, which the ridiculous is if you go up to Mark Zuckerberg and everyone knows what he looks like and who he is and you're like, "Hi, I'm Sam. And who are you?" You're like, "What are you doing?" It's ridiculous. (00:21:55): On the other hand, going up and being like, "You're the most important person I've ever met." Is wrong. And so there's a way to, again, it's about grace as much as anything else and recognizing that they're people. And again, you're playing an iterative game and the best thing you can do is say, as much as it might actually be, this is not my only opportunity to meet Mark. (00:22:14): And in an ideal world when I walk away, I'm like, "That was a pretty nice person. Maybe I want to talk to them again." Now going up and being like, "I need your email address and phone number." It's like, no, let him offer it. That type of stuff I think matters.
turns.zh: 有太多方式了。有一堆关于——我想，笼统说名人——但我说的其实差不多是别阿谀奉承，不过也可以说成别荒唐，如果在这次对话里这么框定的话。荒唐是指：你走到 Mark Zuckerberg 面前——所有人都知道他长什么样、是谁——然后你说：『嗨，我是 Sam。你是哪位？』你心想：『你在干嘛？』这很荒唐。（00:21:55）：另一方面，走过去说你是我见过最重要的人也不对。所以有个方法，再说一次，这关乎 grace，和认识到他们也是人，一样重要。再说一次，你玩的是个 iterative 的游戏，你能做的最好的事就是说——哪怕这真的是事实——『这不是我唯一见到 Mark 的机会。』（00:22:14）：理想情况下，我走开时会想：『那是个挺不错的人。也许我想再和他聊聊。』现在走过去说我要你的邮箱和电话——不行，让他主动给。这类事我觉得重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe one last tip is you actually start with this one of this line of great to see you when you meet someone versus nice to see you again.
turns.zh: 也许最后一条是，你其实是从 great to see you（很高兴见到你）和 nice to see you again（很高兴再次见到你）这条开始的。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Well, again, Lenny, you and I probably use this all the time, I bet, because I honestly, again, we go by name, face, whatever. It's really difficult social situation to put someone in. It just think about from their perspective. If you go up to someone and say, "Hey, it's really great. It's great to meet you. " And you're like, "We've met five times." (00:22:51): It's quite embarrassing and for them, for you, for everyone. And so the more I love ... In fact, my wife of many, many years who have data since college has a really funny story about this, which is the first time right before we started dating, I went up to her and I basically did a nice to see you line and I very clearly couldn't remember if we had met before and we had and she remembered. And so for me, this is an important one to keep in mind.
turns.zh: 看，再说一次，Lenny，我打赌你和我大概一直都在用这句话，因为老实讲，我们都是凭名字、凭脸，管它呢。把人放进那种社交处境真的很尴尬。你只要站在对方角度想想。如果你走到一个人面前说：『嘿，太好了。很高兴认识你。』而对方心里想：『我们都见过五次了。』（00:22:51）：那对人家、对你、对所有人，都挺尴尬的。所以——我越……其实，我和我太太相识于大学、在一起很多很多年了，她有个关于这事儿特别好笑的故事：就在我们开始约会之前的那次，我走到她面前，基本上说了句很高兴见到你，而且我非常明显地记不清我们之前见没见过——而其实我们见过，她也记得。所以对我而言，这是一条要记在心里的重要原则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My wife is constantly making fun of me of saying like, "Oh." And not knowing if I've met someone before not she's like, how can you ... I don't know what to do with you. So that's a great one. So the line there is great to see you because it works whether you meet them or not.
turns.zh: 我太太老是取笑我，说我『哦』一声，然后根本不确定之前见没见过人家，她就：你能怎样……我真拿你没办法。所以这条太棒了。所以那句话就是 great to see you（很高兴见到你），因为不管你见没见过对方，它都管用。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah. And again, it's one of those things where here's the thing. People aren't dumb. If you go around saying nice to see you to everyone, they're like, there's a small percent chance this person doesn't remind me who I ... remember who I am. And there are other ways or cute, but that's okay. That's part of the etiquette dance to some degree is like, that's fine. What's not fine is it's so nice to meet you and we've met six times, right?
turns.zh: 对。再说一次，这种事就是这样——关键在这儿。人不是傻子。如果你见谁都说 nice to see you（很高兴见到你），他们心里会想：这人有很小的概率其实不记得我是谁。也有别的说法、或者可爱的说法，但那都行。在某种程度上，那也是礼仪之舞的一部分，没关系。真正不行的是：我们见过六次了，你却说 so nice to meet you（真高兴认识你），对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep. Okay. Let's talk hygiene. There's a couple there that stood out to me. Tell me if I'm missing any that you think are really important. One is just subtle fragrance.
turns.zh: 对。好。我们来说卫生。那里有几条让我印象很深。如果有什么你觉得特别重要而我漏了的，告诉我。其中一条就是：淡淡的味道。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, don't smell like shit. It's like don't overpower it. You shouldn't smell like you just doused yourself in perfume or cologne or whatever it is, but you also shouldn't smell bad. And it's again, your scent should not be noticeable is almost the way I would put it in any direction. There's no advantage to that is basically what I would say.
turns.zh: 对，身上别一股臭味。就是别让味道压过一切。你不该闻起来像刚把自己泡进香水、古龙水或者随便什么里头，但你也不该有臭味。再说一次，我的说法差不多是：你的气味，无论朝哪个方向，都不该被人注意到。说到底，那样做没有任何好处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: By the way, this is a good question. Does this advice apply both equally to men and women? Is there anything that as maybe as we go through it?
turns.zh: 顺便问，这是个好问题。这些建议对男女都一样适用吗？在我们往下聊的过程中，有没有什么——

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: So it's an interesting question. I think broadly in this book, the answer is broadly yes. I will say that there is probably in January or February going to be a, what we've internally been calling the fem etiquette course because my wife and other women have said, "This is good, but there's a bunch of other stuff that women need to know." And so I can't speak to that yet. I think the fragrance one I would say, I don't think you want your fragrance to be memorable for anyone no matter what your gender is.
turns.zh: 这是个有意思的问题。我觉得大体上在这本书里，答案是大体上『是』。我要说，可能在一月或二月，我们会推出一个我们内部称为女性礼仪课的东西，因为我太太和其他女性都说：『这很好，但有一堆别的东西是女性需要知道的。』所以我暂时还无法谈那个。我觉得关于味道那条，我想说的是：无论你什么性别，你都不该让你的气味被任何人记住。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. This is good. Let me take two tangents here real quick. One is, you told a story on your podcast about your kids and the impact this has had on them. Maybe share a story there.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这很好。让我快速扯两个题外话。一个是，你在自己播客里讲过一个关于你孩子、以及这事对他们影响的故事。也许在那儿分享一下。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Well, look, here's the funny thing. I literally have realized in doing this, I love my children. They have terrible manners and there's certain things they're not bad at. But broadly speaking, I have an eight-year-old, a six-year-old, and a four-year-old. And I'm like, "Wow, you guys eat like animals. You don't know how to use a forklift knife properly." Again, it's not like at four or six, it's not like stopping them well in life. I'm like, "I can't be the etiquette guy if you guys are eating like." Some of them has been really cute. (00:25:37): Others have been really funny. My six-year-old has started standing whenever my wife comes to the table, which is kind of arcane from an etiquette perspective. You can argue about whether it's actually even really etiquette anymore or not. But if you're being really formal when a woman comes to the table, you stand. And it's very funny to have the six-year-old do that. So in our household-
turns.zh: 看，好笑的事在这儿。做这件事的过程中，我真的意识到，我爱我的孩子们。他们的礼仪糟透了，不过有些事他们也不算差。但总的来说，我有个八岁的、一个六岁的、还有一个四岁的。我就想：『哇，你们吃东西像动物。你们连刀叉都还不会好好用。』再说一次，在四岁或六岁这个年纪，倒也不至于就耽误了他们的人生。我就想：『如果你们吃饭这副样子，我就当不了那个礼仪先生了。』他们有些表现真的可爱。（00:25:37）：另一些真的好笑。我六岁的儿子，现在每当太太走到餐桌前，就会站起来——从礼仪角度讲这有点古老了。你可以争论这如今还算不算真礼仪。但如果你真的很正式，当一位女性走到桌前，你会起立。而让一个六岁小孩这么做，真的很好笑。所以在我们家——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so funny.
turns.zh: 那太好笑了。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Don't judge me yet, but in a year you can judge me on my children's etiquette. Then it might have to be a children's etiquette book.
turns.zh: 现在先别评判我，不过一年后你可以就我孩子们的礼仪来评判我。到时候说不定得出一本儿童礼仪书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So good. I think actually at the end you say that whenever anyone joins you for meal, whether it's a man or woman, you stand up as a modern way of thinking about that.
turns.zh: 太好了。我记得其实在结尾你说过，无论谁来和你一起吃饭，不管是男是女，你都会站起来——作为一种现代的思考方式。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: That might be better is what I would say. I will say that it's an ongoing, somewhat hilarious debate at our dinner table. I'm just trying to get them to not use a fork and knife like animals right now, but we're working on it. We're working on it.
turns.zh: 我想说，那样也许更好。我要说，这在我们餐桌上是个持续进行、有点好笑的争论。我现在只是想让他们别像动物一样用叉子和刀，不过我们在努力。我们在努力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just speaking of that. I was just listening to Tyler Cowen had Alison Gopnik on this podcast and she studies kids and her whole thing is how kids learn scientists and she has a whole thing about how they figure out how to use a fork by just experimenting until something works.
turns.zh: 我刚说到这个。我刚在听 Tyler Cowen 的播客，请了 Alison Gopnik，她研究小孩，她的整套观点是关于小孩如何像科学家一样学习，而且她有一整套说法，讲小孩是怎么通过不断尝试、直到某样东西管用，来搞明白怎么用叉子的。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Right. To be clear, they're able to feed themselves. It works, but it's like you look at it and it's like, what are you doing?
turns.zh: 对。说清楚，他们是能自己喂饱自己的。那管用，但你看着那个画面，就会想：你到底在干嘛？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. The other tangent is you didn't share the class you actually taught to founders already. So maybe share a little bit about this class you taught.
turns.zh: 对。好。另一个题外话是，你还没分享你实际上已经给创始人开过的那堂课。所以也许稍微分享一下你开的这堂课。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah. So before the book, we did a class specifically initially for YC founders, right? Partially because YC, Garry Tan got very mad about this. So I'm like, well, now I have to do it because that's very funny. But yeah, we basically, we gave them all certificates of completion, but we did a class. We hosted, it was at the Four Seasons. We did some stuff that was fun and a little bit irreverent. (00:27:10): We had some very fancy wokes basher people come in with models and show a talk about dress at different types of events and things like that, which was kind of tongue in cheek, but a lot of fun. We also did caviar and wine tasting type stuff. But then we also spent a lot of time focusing on the actual meat of the matter, which is things like how to show up with a low heart rate, how to have an abundance mindset, basic skills, like look people with the eye, shaking hands, how to eat that shows that you're being respectful, things like that.
turns.zh: 对。所以在出书之前，我们先开了一堂课，最初是专门给 YC 的创始人开的，对吧？部分原因是 YC 的 Garry Tan 为此特别生气。所以我就想，好吧，那我现在非做不可了，因为那很好笑。不过没错，我们基本是给他们都发了结业证书，但我们确实开了一堂课。我们主办，地点在四季酒店。我们搞了一些好玩、又有点不羁的东西。（00:27:10）：我们请了一些非常时髦的、搞穿搭的人带着模特进来，做了个关于不同场合怎么穿之类的演讲，有点半开玩笑，但很好玩。我们还搞了鱼子酱和品酒之类的环节。但然后我们也花大量时间聚焦在真正的实质问题上，比如如何心平气和地登场、如何拥有丰盈心态，以及基本技能，比如用眼神看人、握手、怎么吃才显得你有尊重之意，诸如此类。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Why do you think Garry Tan was so mad at it? Is it because he's like, "This is a waste of time, not worth it." Versus just build a thing that's successful?
turns.zh: 你觉得 Garry Tan 为什么那么生气？是因为他觉得『这是在浪费时间、不值得』，而不是去打造一个成功的产品？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I don't know. I don't really understand what makes Garry Tan mad and it's fine. But from my perspective, I think he's just like, in some ways, again, to be clear, it's a little tongue in cheek. We're a little bit making fun of the fact that YC Founders do come out a little bit like animals. Having met with many of them, I guess it's not their fault. (00:28:01): They're like young kids, they've been holed up in a room coding and that's all they've been thinking about for months or whatever. And so when they show up at your office to pitch you and they get a coffee or something and then they leave it on the table and don't ask you where to put it, it's a subtle sign of not being aware of your broader environment that you may or may not know, but I think it's valuable. Maybe they're like, "This is the wrong thing to focus on." I just think it's funny as much as anything else.
turns.zh: 我不知道。我其实不太懂是什么让 Garry Tan 生气，不过没关系。但从我的角度，我觉得他差不多就是——再说一次，说清楚，这有点半开玩笑。我们多少是在拿『YC 的创始人出来的时候确实有点像动物』这个事实开涮。我见过他们很多人的面，我想那不是他们的错。（00:28:01）：他们就像年轻小孩，一直闷在房间里写代码，好几个月来满脑子就只想着这个。所以当他们出现在你办公室向你 pitch，拿了杯咖啡之类的，然后把它留在桌上，也不问你该放哪儿，这就是一个微妙的信号，表明他们没意识到更广阔的环境——你也许知道、也许不知道，但我觉得这很有价值。也许他们会想：『这是不该聚焦的错事。』但我只是觉得，这和其他任何事一样，挺好笑的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Okay. So on the hygiene thing, is there anything else?
turns.zh: 我爱死这个了。好。那在卫生这块，还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I think the hygiene stuff, you should get the book. I think it's fairly obvious hygiene stuff. Don't be covered in schmutz, you know what I mean? Show respect, try to anticipate how the room is going to be dressed and don't massively overdress or underdress. It's like if you show up to a business casual thing in a tuxedo, you're kind of trying to stand out. Don't be memorable from that perspective, but you also don't want to be memorable in the other direction. It's like, "Wow, that person really has no respect for the room."
turns.zh: 我觉得卫生这块，你该去买这本书。我觉得都是挺明显的卫生常识。身上别沾满脏东西，你懂我意思吧？表现出尊重，试着预判房间里的人会怎么穿，别穿得过于隆重或过于随便。就好比，如果你穿着燕尾服出现在商务休闲的场合，你有点像在故意出风头。从那个角度，别让人记住你，但从另一个方向，你也别让人记住。就像：『哇，那人真的一点都不尊重这个场合。』

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This actually, you're getting to the next category, which is dress, which I'm excited about.
turns.zh: 这其实就已经引到下一个类别了，也就是穿着，这个我挺兴奋的。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah. Look, I got to say, again, in terms of know the rules, but don't always follow them. My first job out of college, I was an associate at a bathing company. This is a consulting firm and there was a business casual and I kind of came up with the snarky realization that there was a minimum dress code, but there wasn't a maximum dress code. So I started in the office as somewhat of a mini rebellion in the consulting firm, what we call tuxedo Tuesdays, where all the associates would wear tuxedos to work, which then meant we didn't have to go to the client meetings because they would never take us to client meetings and tuxedos. (00:29:32): So it was like, again, you know the rules to break them, it was fun. But I do think from a dress perspective, again, I think the real thing is look put together, look like you cared, look like you made some effort, but you don't overdo it is basically the upshot of the most simple way to dress, unless you're trying to very intentionally break a rule, which maybe you are, but I think you should do that with a lot of cultural understanding. Let's put it that way.
turns.zh: 对。看，我得说，再说一次，就『懂规则，但不总照做』而言。我大学毕业后的第一份工作，是在一家 bathing 公司当 associate。那是一家咨询公司，当时是商务休闲着装，而我有点刻薄地意识到：有最低着装要求，却没有最高着装要求。于是作为对咨询公司某种小小的反叛，我在办公室发起了一个我们叫做燕尾服星期二的活动，所有 associate 都穿燕尾服上班，这就导致我们不用去见客户了，因为他们绝不会带着穿燕尾服的人去见客户。（00:29:32）：所以就像，再说一次，你懂规则是为了打破它们，这很好玩。但我确实觉得，从穿着角度，再说一次，真正的关键是：看起来整洁利落、看起来你在意、看起来你花过心思，但别做过头——这基本就是最简单穿法的最终要义。除非你是非常刻意地想去打破某条规则，也许你确实想，但我觉得你该带着充分的文化理解去做。就这么定吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So here's a couple tips that I love. So one is just dress one Level up as a really simple tip.
turns.zh: 那我来说几个我超爱的建议。其中一个就是：穿着比场合高一个 level，这是个特别简单的建议。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's an easy way to win. Not two, not three, but one.
turns.zh: 这是轻松获胜的办法。不是一个 level、两个 level，而是一个 level。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And oftentimes you can reduce that. If you have a suit on, you could take off the jacket and you're a little less formal.
turns.zh: 而且很多时候你可以降下来。如果你穿着西装，你可以脱掉外套，就没那么正式了。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Sure. 100%.
turns.zh: 当然。百分之百。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then you talk about fit of the item versus the brand.
turns.zh: 然后你聊到单品的合身度，而非品牌。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: 100%. At the end of the day, fit is everything. And I say this, again, you guys, all your listeners have to understand. Part of my joy at doing this is there's some level of hypocrisy in it, which is great. You got to have a little bit of that in your life in terms of how I myself behave sometimes. But look, in the end of the day, a well-fitting $20 shirt is way better than a misfitting $500 shirt. (00:30:41): And candidly, it's the same thing. It's like if you're a startup founder, you do want to dress to the level of the room, but you kind of shouldn't show up and you shouldn't have a Rolex. It's very classless, if that makes sense, to show up as a startup founder with a Rolex. Again, it goes back to heart rates, trying too hard. You're not going to trick anyone is the upshot.
turns.zh: 百分之百。说到底，合身就是一切。我再强调一下，你们所有听众都得明白。我做这事的一大乐趣，是这里面有某种程度的 hypocrisy，而这很好。就我自己的某些行为而言，你的人生里总得有点这种东西。但看，说到底，一件合身的 20 美元衬衫，远胜过一件不合身的 500 美元衬衫。（00:30:41）：而且坦白讲，道理是一样的。就好比，如果你是个创业公司创始人，你确实想穿得和这个场合的 level 匹配，但你不该那么登场，你也不该戴个 Rolex。作为创业公司创始人戴着 Rolex 出现，如果这说得通的话，是非常没品味的。再说一次，这又回到心率、回到用力过猛。结论是：你骗不了任何人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. This bit of our brand and just expensiveness of the item is such a big one that I think is ... I think people don't realize just it could be a pretty cheap thing that if you get tailored in some small way, it just looks so much better even if it's not the highest quality item.
turns.zh: 对。这一条关于『品牌和单品贵不贵』的，是个很大的点，我觉得……我觉得人们没意识到，哪怕是很便宜的东西，只要稍微改个尺寸，看起来就会好太多，哪怕它质量不是最顶级的。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: A hundred percent. Again, I would put differently, think about the average person, not every person in the world, but the average person in the world can look at a suit and be like intuitively that seems like it fits the person who doesn't. Most people can have no idea what things cost. And so in some ways, it's this weird thing where it's like if you show up at a super misfitting but very expensive item, you're like, "What signal are you setting?" (00:31:47): It's like, well, you're not very aware culturally. You're not matching the room. You're not showing a lot of sensitivity to the situation and what people actually can prioritize. And it's like, are you trying to impress me because you have a fancy outfit? What are we talking about?
turns.zh: 百分之百。再说一次，我会换个说法：想想普通人——不是全世界每个人，但世界上普通人——看一套西装，直觉上能判断它合不合身。大多数人根本不知道东西花了多少钱。所以在某种意义上，这挺诡异的：如果你穿着一件超级不合身、却很贵的单品出现，你就像在说：『你到底在发出什么信号？』（00:31:47）：就好像，嗯，你在文化上不太敏锐。你没有和这个场合匹配。你没有对情境、以及人们真正能优先看重的东西表现出足够的敏感度。就好像，你是想靠一身华丽的行头去打动我吗？我们到底在说啥？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One other tip you have is if you're not sure the level of dress, just ask.
turns.zh: 你还有一条建议是：如果你不确定该穿多正式，就直接问。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, this is a big thing in general, which is I think people are afraid to ask in all sorts of situations down to which forks should I use? Or what's the expect? It is absolutely fine to ask. In fact, if anything, it shows a level of confidence and calm and humility to ask if you don't know. So I actually think this is a great example. There's absolutely nothing wrong with asking about dress, about etiquette, about expectations. Again, it goes back to this whole give to get. (00:32:35): If you get someone on the phone and you ask them a hundred questions about etiquette, at a certain point you're like, that's not a pit game of ping pong. But it's totally fine to call and be like, "Hey, what's this going to look like?" And by the way, it's important because in New York versus San Francisco, there's different expectations. People do things differently and your job, you're not expected to know every nuance of every culture you might enter.
turns.zh: 对，这是一件普遍的大事，我觉得人们在各种情境下都害怕问，小到该用哪把叉子？或者该期待什么？问，绝对没问题。事实上，如果有什么的话，当你不懂时去问，反而展现出一种自信、冷静和谦逊。所以我其实觉得这是个很好的例子。询问穿着、询问礼仪、询问期待，绝对没有半点错。再说一次，这又回到整个『有来有往』。（00:32:35）：如果你在电话里跟人问了一百个关于礼仪的问题，到某个点你会想：那可不是一场漂亮的乒乓球赛。但打电话说『嘿，这事儿大概会是什么样？』完全没问题。而且顺便说，这很重要，因为在纽约对比旧金山，人们的期待不同。大家做法不一样，而你的任务——没人要求你知晓你可能进入的每种文化的每一个细微差别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So maybe as a final question in dress, do you have any just, I don't know, tips for dressing well? I know this is a big question that our professionals spend time teaching and charging for.
turns.zh: 那也许作为穿着部分的最后一个问题：你有没有什么——我不知道——把衣服穿好看的建议？我知道这是个很大的问题，专业形象顾问都要花时间教学、收费的。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I think the answer is find someone in your universe who you think dresses well. And again, ask them for help and what makes sense from that perspective. Again, the well-tailored, great. That makes a lot of sense. The basics I can say, yeah, have jeans that are clean and fit you, things like that. But again, when my wife listens to this podcast episode and hears me being asked about specifics of dress, she's going to be chuckling.
turns.zh: 我想答案是：在你自己的圈子里，找一个你觉得穿得好的人。再说一次，请他们帮忙，从这个角度去想什么合理。再说一次，改得合身，很好。那很有道理。基本面上我能说的是：嗯，有干净、合身的牛仔裤，诸如此类。但再说一次，当我太太听到这期播客、听到我被问到穿着的具体细节，她会偷笑的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. That's a win. Okay. Let's talk about dining. Give us some advice for etiquette during dining.
turns.zh: 好。那算赢了一局。好。我们来说用餐。给我们一些用餐时的礼仪建议。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Tip well. Don't not tip, don't tip badly. Don't be super stingy about, "Okay, who ordered the flambe?" Split bills evenly, make things easy for waiters. In general, it's don't order the most expensive thing on the menu. Does it really matter? Especially to an investor, do they really care? No, they don't really care, but they do notice. And you're like, ah, you are the type of person that is truly insensitive to what things cost, even if it doesn't actually matter, and so I think there are things like that. (00:34:25): Same with wine. And then I think, look, in the terms of asking, ideally, don't order first because I think if you see how someone ... Are we doing starters? How long is this meal going to be? There's a lot of times in dining situations you don't know. And the more you let someone else set the tone and then match that tone, the better. You kind of want to go middle of the pack to last, if that makes sense. Yeah.
turns.zh: 给好小费。别不给、也别给得太少。别在『好吧，谁点了那道火焰甜点？』这种事上吝啬到极点。账单平分，让服务员省心。总的来说，就是别点菜单上最贵的东西。这真的有关系吗？尤其对投资人，他们真的在意吗？不，他们其实不在乎，但他们确实会注意到。然后你就会想：啊，你是那种对价格真正无感的人，哪怕这其实无所谓——所以我觉得就有这类事。（00:34:25）：酒也是一样。然后我觉得，看，就『问』这个角度，理想情况下，别第一个点单。因为我觉得，如果你先看别人怎么……我们要点前菜吗？这顿饭要持续多久？用餐情境里很多时候你是不知道的。你越让别人定调、然后你去匹配那个调子，越好。你大概想处在队伍中间到靠后的位置，如果这说得通的话。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this isn't a situation if someone takes you out to dinner, like it's a VC, another found, someone invites you to dinner.
turns.zh: 所以这不是说，如果是别人请你吃晚饭——比如一个风投、另一个创始人、某人邀你吃饭——的情况。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Or a partner or whatever it is.
turns.zh: 或者一个合伙人，管它是什么呢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Awesome.
turns.zh: 对。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: And look, I think I would say in terms of this, which I always think is important is like, look, within reason, always offer to pay. Now, you should be turned down. If you go out with a VC and you put a card down, 99% of the time they'll be like, "I got this. Please, don't worry about it." And that's the right vibe on it. You do not need to do this if it's a $10,000 dinner, if they've ordered a super expensive bottle of wine. (00:35:25): There are limits to this, but if you go out to a normal dinner in a normal situation, you don't offer to split it, you just offer to pay for it. And then you should be declined on that, but there is a little bit of a risk there because someone might not decline you and then you kind of are on the hook for it, but that is, I think, the polite thing and the polite way to approach it.
turns.zh: 看，我觉得就这点我想说的是，我一直觉得重要的事是：在合理范围内，永远主动提出由你买单。现在，你应该被拒绝。如果你和风投出去，你刷了卡，99% 的情况下他们会说：『我来付。拜托，别操心。』那才是正确的氛围。如果是一顿 1 万美元的晚餐、如果他们点了一瓶超级贵的酒，你就没必要这么做了。（00:35:25）：这事是有限度的，但如果你在正常的情境下外出吃一顿正常的饭，你不该提议平分，你只该主动提出由你付全款。然后你应该被拒绝，但这里有点风险，因为对方可能不拒绝你，那你就得掏钱了——但我觉得，那才是礼貌的做法、礼貌的处理方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What if they're just a billionaire? I just had dinner with a very successful VC and I did not feel like offering to pay made sense, would you still-
turns.zh: 如果他们就是个亿万富翁呢？我刚和一位非常成功的风投吃了饭，我觉得主动提出买单不太合理，你还会——

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, I actually would. I think it depends what the dynamic is. If the billionaire ordered a $10,000 bottle of wine, you don't need to offer. If you had a normal meal, I actually think it's great to offer. And they'll almost certainly be like, "Of course not." But I will say, I'll tell you a funny story, which is when you go out with dinner to really fancy people or someone who's like ... There are two interesting dynamics. (00:36:19): One is it's actually, I think, especially nice to offer and even sometimes pay because the reality is, if you think about it, they obviously don't care about the money, but no one does that. They're like, "Well, clearly you should pay." And so the more you're like, "Oh no, I'm treating us like this is a conversation and equals and I'd love to offer or just pay as big." (00:36:38): The second thing, which is important is if you're, especially if you're out to dinner with someone who's very, very well known, you have to tip like crazy because the problem is, this is one thing, this is not in the book, this is a 201 course. But if you go out and start with someone that are like, okay, they're either known or relatively known known and you're making the gesture of buying it, not because they obviously don't care about the money. (00:37:01): It's more like the gesture that's nice that you would offer that. You kind of have to tip the way they would tip and they're going to tip 100% of the bill because it's just the right thing to do. And so I do think if you're going to do that, you really have to tip well.
turns.zh: 对，我其实还是会。我觉得这取决于具体的动态。如果那位亿万富翁点了一瓶 1 万美元的酒，你没必要提议。如果你们吃的是一顿普通的饭，我其实觉得主动提出来特别好。而且他们几乎肯定会说：『当然不用。』但我要说，我给你讲个好笑的故事：当你和真正讲究的人、或者某种……出去吃饭时，有两种有趣的动态。（00:36:19）：其一，我觉得，主动提出、甚至有时真的付钱，其实特别好，因为现实是，你想想就知道，他们显然不在乎钱，但没人会这么做。他们会想：『嗯，显然该你付。』所以你越是说『哦不，这顿我请，就当这是场对话、我们是平等的，我很乐意提议、或者直接大方地付』，（00:36:38）：第二件重要的事是：尤其当你和某个非常、非常有名的人出去吃饭，你得像疯了一样给小费。因为问题在这儿——这是一件事，书里没写，这是 201 进阶课。但如果你和某个——好吧，他们要么很有名、要么相对有名——出去，并且你做出要买单的姿态，不是因为他们显然不在乎钱，（00:37:01）：更像是：你愿意主动提出来，这个姿态本身很体贴。你多少得按他们会给小费的方式来给，而他们会按账单的 100% 给，因为那本就是该做的事。所以我确实觉得，如果你要那么做，你就真得给足小费。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Speaking of tipping, my God, I hate tipping so much as a concept. Obviously, people deserve to be paid well and I love that they make more money, but it's just so convoluted and just like, what the hell do I do? I never know.
turns.zh: 明白了。说到小费，我的天，我作为概念极其讨厌小费。显然，服务员值得拿到好报酬，我也乐见他们赚更多钱，但这太绕了，就，我到底该干嘛？我从来不知道。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Tip a lot.
turns.zh: 给很多小费。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tip a lot. Okay.
turns.zh: 给很多小费。好。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Just tip a lot. I think 10, 20% is the minimum. If you're out in a situation, I think you kind of want to tip in my mind to the level of no one you're effectively paying for would bat an eye that you're being stingy is the way I would think about it. 20% feels like the minimum. 30% sometimes, more seems a little bit silly, but it is a squirrely topic. And again, let me put it this way. I don't think you want your tip to be memorable is almost way to put it. (00:38:01): This is not a thing to focus on. When the person that go out to dinner with thinks back on the dinner a month later, they want to think about the content of the conversation or what the ideas were or the business opportunity, they want to think about, "Oh my God, that guy tipped an incredible amount. What was that?" (00:38:17): And by the way, I have stories in my own life where I've been out with people and they've tipped so much that a decade later I remember it. And I'm like, "It's fine. They can afford it." It's cool that they did that for the server, but honestly, the only thing I remember from the night is how much the person tips.
turns.zh: 就是给很多小费。我觉得 10%、20% 是最低限度。如果你在外面那种场合，我觉得在我心里，你给小费的程度，应该到你实际在付钱的那个人不会因你吝啬而眨一下眼——我是这么想的。20% 感觉像是最低。30% 有时也行，再多就有点傻了，但这是个棘手的话题。再说一次，让我这么说：我觉得你不该让你的小费被人记住，差不多该这么理解。（00:38:01）：这不是该聚焦的事。当一个和你出去吃过饭的人，一个月后回想起那顿饭，他们想的是对话的内容、那些想法、或者那个商业机会，而不是想：『我的天，那家伙给了笔惊人的小费，那是什么鬼？』（00:38:17）：而且顺便说，我自己的生活里就有这种故事：我和某些人出去，他们小费给得那么多，十年后我都记得。而我就会想：『没事，他们付得起。』他们为服务员那么做，挺酷的，但老实说，那一晚我唯一记得的，就是那人给了多少小费。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. But I think if you're extremely rich, you do it. Don't even tell anyone basically, but feel free to do it, obviously.
turns.zh: 好。但我觉得如果你极其有钱，你就该那么做。基本别告诉任何人，但显然，尽管去做。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Sure. Yeah. The tip is not a point. The tip is like everyone should feel good about it. And again, it's about, again, putting people in a sense of ease and comfort and you might not like it and it might not be fair in the world, but people are like, everyone's being taken care of. I can be relaxed about this is kind of what you're going for.
turns.zh: 当然。对。小费不是个得分点。小费是说，每个人都该对此感觉良好。再说一次，这关乎让人感到安心和舒适，你可能不喜欢它、它在世上也许不公平，但人们会想：大家都被照顾到了。我可以对此放松——这差不多就是你要追求的状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I recommend your next book after this FamiKit edition is a tipping guide.
turns.zh: 我建议你在这本 FamiKit 版之后，下一本书出个给小费的指南。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: A tipping guide. Well, you know what would be funny is there's a great episode of Seinfeld that's all about the tipping calculator. I don't know if you're a Seinfeld guy.
turns.zh: 给小费的指南。嗯，你知道什么会很好笑吗？《宋飞正传》里有一集特别棒，全是关于小费计算器的。不知道你是不是看宋飞的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love Seinfeld. I don't remember that.
turns.zh: 我爱《宋飞正传》。我不记得那一集了。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's a great tipping episode. I feel like you could honestly have a very funny modern LLM app that is only about tipping. Imagine a tipping app where instead of a tipping calculator, you take a picture of the bill, it geolocates where you are, you're like, "This is the situation." And it just tells you what to tip.
turns.zh: 那是集很棒的小费集。我觉得你真可以做一个特别好笑的现代 LLM 应用，只关于小费。想象一个 tipping 应用：不用小费计算器，你拍张账单照片，它地理定位你在哪儿，你说：『这就是当时的情形。』然后它就告诉你该给多少小费。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, a restaurant is one thing, but then it's like the garbage person, a gardener, the person that-
turns.zh: 嗯，餐厅是一回事，但接着就是收垃圾的、园丁、那个——

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Especially this time, end of year, at the end of year-
turns.zh: 尤其这个时节，年底——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，正是。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I think no one knows how to tip anymore.
turns.zh: 我觉得现在没人知道该怎么给小费了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, some guy that installs the shades in our house. Do I tip?
turns.zh: 对，就是来我家装遮阳帘的那个师傅。我要给小费吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I don't think you tip that person. Do you tip that person?
turns.zh: 我觉得你不该给那人小费。你会给那人小费吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I did not because you already paid a bunch of money for this thing.
turns.zh: 不，我没给，因为你已经为这玩意儿付了一大笔钱了。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, no, I feel like that is weird. I wouldn't tip people like that.
turns.zh: 对，不，我觉得那很怪。我不会给那种人小费。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's why we need this book. You're just going to be a huge hit. What does [inaudible 00:40:08]?
turns.zh: 这就是我们为什么需要这本书。你就快火了。 [inaudible 00:40:08] 是什么意思？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Why are you going to fund it? You want to fund it with me? We should fund an app. Talk about YC companies. If someone pitched me in the terms of funny but real, if someone pitched me the 2026 AI-driven tipping calculator, which gives the social situation and the details and all the things and it's like, this is how much to tip, that is hilarious and probably quite useful.
turns.zh: 你为什么要给它出钱？你想跟我一起投它？我们该投个应用。说到 YC 公司。如果有人以那种好笑但真实的方式向我 pitch，如果有人拿一个 2026 年 AI 驱动的小费计算器来 pitch 我——它会给出社交情境、细节、所有那些东西，然后说该给这么多小费——那会很好笑，而且大概相当有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And probably not venture scale, but I don't care.
turns.zh: 而且大概到不了风投的规模，但我不在乎。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: You know what? It's 2026, it might be. Everyone has the problem. Everyone globally has the same problem, which is tipping.
turns.zh: 你知道吗？都 2026 年了，说不定它能。人人都有这问题。全球每个人都有着同样的问题，就是小费。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, just the tokens cost of that.
turns.zh: 对，光是那个的 token 成本。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It actually reminds me, I'm reading one of my sons right now, the third book of Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
turns.zh: 这其实让我想起，我现在正给我一个儿子读《银河系搭便车指南》的第三本。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯哼。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: And I don't know if you've read this series.
turns.zh: 不知道你读没读过这个系列。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 读过。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's important stuff. Do you remember about the, what's Bristomatics Mathics?
turns.zh: 这很重要。你还记得那个吗，Bristomatics Mathics 是什么来着？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不记得了。

turns.zh: 哦，BD。你只要看自己的手，对吧？B 和 D，也就是你的面包盘在哪边——差不多是该这么想。而且看，人们一直在这上面搞错。你坐在一张大桌子前，就会想：啊，哪个是我的？然后你有点在等别人先拿起、好算出来。我就会想：『好，那是我的面包。』但 B 和 D 很有用。还有，看，刀叉，只要知道它们该放哪边就行；还有一件老是让我抓狂的、相关的细节：刀刃要朝里。（00:42:11）：人们放下刀的时候，刀刃要朝里，因为你不想戳到旁边的同伴，但这真的很好笑。我有个创业者——这还没变成产品——人们开始给我发他们用餐或在各种场合的视频，让我给反馈。我最近就给一位创业者反馈，他说：『你汤喝得真不错。干得好。你的餐巾本该放在腿上，而且你的刀尖朝错方向了。』

turns.zh: 我觉得你不该让你的餐巾摆放被人记住。我最核心的一点是：礼仪的意义在于它让一切顺当通过，不挡路。它不该被人记住。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Here's the thing. Humor's great. I love humor. It can be overdone. And again, it shouldn't be the point of things. And also, I'd say humor is quite conditional and subtle to the audience. (00:43:40): If you're able to tell a joke, which is right up to the line or even pushes at one degree to show your own comfort in the space. So if you're really in it and feeling good, using humor is great. (00:44:02): You should not be remembered as only the comedian. turns.zh: 关键在这儿。幽默很好。我爱幽默。但它可能做过头。再说一次，它不该成为事情的重点。而且，我会说，幽默对受众而言是相当有条件、相当微妙的。所以在你所处的房间里，脏笑话——你不该在错误的房间讲脏笑话。但我觉得关于幽默有意思的微妙之处在于，为什么它在社交场合这么有用：其一，它在某种程度上展示了你对一个社交情境的终极掌控。（00:43:40）：如果你能讲一个笑话，正好压线、甚至越线一度，来展示你在这个空间里的自在——所以在一个空间里自在的终极示范，就是讲一个稍微越线、或者稍微有点颜色的笑话，但不能太颜色。那差不多就是终极的东西。所以如果你真的沉浸其中、感觉很好，用幽默就很好。（00:44:02）：你不该只被记住是个喜剧演员。再说一次，你在玩的笑话的程度，是件非常微妙的事。所以你不该给成年人讲敲门笑话，但那个好笑的、有点颜色的性笑话，你在讲之前最好相当有把握。你最不想要的，是大家都笑的笑话当然好，（00:44:28）：但没人笑的笑话，就像你搞砸了一次巨大的冒险举动。那不是重点。所以它是个好工具。我爱它。我觉得每个人都该有自己的笑话档案。我有。我不知道你有没有，但我有一个 Evernote。现在不是 Evernote 了。像是放我最爱笑话的一个 bear。它们大致按从最不冒犯到最冒犯排了序，因为我会忘掉笑话，但你多少该节制而聪明地用幽默。

turns.zh: 对，你想准备一些轻松的小故事。再说一次，它们不该讲十分钟。但再说一次，我觉得关键是：想象在这些社交场合里，整场游戏——再说一次——是让他人放松，让他们觉得你理解他们、理解这个房间，而且你是个可信、跟他们对上了波长的人。在某种程度上，把它想成：是谁在撑着这场对话？（00:47:25）：它不该是你的独白。你也不该逼他们独白。这就回到了一问一答、有来有往。准备一个好玩的、可以搭起来的故事，他们讲一个，你也有一个可讲。再说一次，我真的把这些对话、这些社交互动，当成一场乒乓球赛，而你多少该在武器库里备上几个这样的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your last tip in that section was how to wind down a conversation, just the importance of realizing it's time to wind down any tips for how to do that.
turns.zh: 你在那部分最后一条建议是关于如何收尾一场对话——就是意识到该收尾了的重要性。有什么关于怎么做的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah. Just like when the conversation is over, gracefully leave and basically the upshot. (00:48:09): Most of the time, that is not an invitation saying, "I'd love one too and follow them to the bar." turns.zh: 对。就像当对话结束时，优雅地离开，这基本就是要义。最糟的是对话结束了，那人却只是站在那儿，你心想：『我去拿杯喝的。』你懂我意思吧？然后偶尔，如果有人在对你说我把它收尾了，就像：『我去拿杯喝的。』（00:48:09）：大多数时候，那不是一种邀请、说我也来一杯，跟你一起去吧台。所以我只是觉得，你得有效地识别那些信号——当那一刻正在过去、或者该继续往前走了等等——然后尊重它，这是我想说的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I use that one all the time. Is there any other ways you find useful to wind down in conversation just to get out of a conversation?
turns.zh: 我老用这一招。你还有别的、觉得有用的收尾方式，纯粹就是为了从一场对话里脱身吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin

In some ways, give them their next partner and be like, "Oh, I've enjoyed this conversation. It's super cool. By the way, have you met Steve? Let's go meet Steve. Go talk to Steve for a bit and I'll pick you back on it." And like, "Okay, I'm going to go say hi to my wife." (00:48:55): There's ways to handle it. Again, the key though is subtlety on these things, I think in all things. You want to basically let people feel respected as much as anything else. So if you're too overt about it, even if everyone kind of knows what's going on, the key is to give them plausible deniability to themselves and the community effectively that we've wound down this conversation. So you have to look for the signs.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得人们经常做的另一件事——再说一次，只要做得尊重，就完全没问题——是把别人带进对话里。在某种程度上，给他们下一个搭子，像说：『哦，我很享受这场对话。太酷了。对了，你见过 Steve 吗？我们去见 Steve 吧。去和 Steve 聊会儿，我等下再回来找你。』然后像：『好，我去跟我太太打个招呼。』（00:48:55）：有办法处理这个。再说一次，不过关键是这些事上的微妙，我觉得凡事都如此。你基本上想让人感到被尊重，这比什么都重要。所以如果你做得太露骨，哪怕大家都大概知道怎么回事，关键是给他们——以及这个圈子——一种合情合理的推诿空间，让这场对话已经收尾了。所以你得留意那些信号。
