Look, rescheduling happens when you do it, give notice as much as possible. (00:50:55): Once you're asking for rescheduling, you need to be even more accepting of what the other person can do, I think is really important. If you're asking to reschedule, you basically within reason need to make it work for them, is what I would say. And then look, I think there's obvious stuff that people should know and sometimes forget. Time zones are really tricky. People screw them up all the time. Check. (00:51:17): It's worth the extra check to make sure you're not both scheduling, you're getting the numbers right, but then also really importantly, scheduling at reasonable times. Sometimes people are like, "I want to meet at this time." You're on EST, you're aware, that's like 4:00 in the morning for me. And so I think being respectful of that and just asking, I think is super important. (00:51:34): It's not rocket science because it's important. Last point I make, which we make in the book is you really need to respect EAs and PAs and the whole people. The number one way to look extremely classless is to not respect people who are helping the other person. This is the number one thing. Now you don't need to be so over the top exuberant. (00:51:57): You don't want to overdo it, but there should be this deep well of respect for anyone who's helping you, whether that's a server or a PA or an EA or whatever. This needs to come with an extra gesture of respect. That means saying thank you when they schedule and follow up with them and things like that.
turns.zh: 没有坏宣传，也没有坏推文。对。所以我觉得，看，有几个明显的。确保你有空档。如果你请别人和你约时间，说这是我的空档或者这是链接，并不总错。但要让它是真的。你得给他们真正的选项。我非常强烈地认为，默认不该是 Calendly。（00:50:13）：在大多数情境下的默认——尤其当你意识到权力位阶或忙碌位阶时。如果你是资历较浅的人，如果你是较不忙的人，你应该让对方告诉你他们何时有空，然后你这头去配合，这是我想说的。第一次提议不成没关系，但前三回里总得有一回成。（00:50:33）：所以我觉得，在某种程度上，尊重这一点很重要。更好的做法是问他们能怎么做，然后挪动你的日程。如果你真的挪不动、打算用个排程助手之类的，它基本上得真的有真实选项——我觉得这总是冒出来。看，改期这种事，当你要改的时候，尽量提前通知。（00:50:55）：一旦你在请求改期，我觉得你就需要更包容对方能怎么做——这真的很重要。如果你在请求改期，基本上在合理范围内，你得让它对对方行得通，这是我想说的。然后看，我觉得有些显而易见、人们该知道却有时忘记的东西。时区真的很棘手。人们一直搞错。核对一下。（00:51:17）：多核对一次是值得的，确保你们不是在两边都排了、数字也对，但同样真正重要的是，排在合理的时间。有时人们会说：『我想在这个时间见面。』你在东部时间，你 aware，那对我来说是凌晨 4 点。所以我觉得尊重这一点、并且直接问，超级重要。（00:51:34）：这不是火箭科学……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'll tell a story when we were selling our company to Airbnb, we had this guy helping us sell the company and he made it a big point to build a good relationship with the EA and office manager at Airbnb because if they like you, it helps. It helps you get the thing.
turns.zh: 我讲个故事：我们当时把公司卖给 Airbnb，有个家伙帮我们卖公司，他特别用心地和 Airbnb 的 EA 和办公室主任搞好关系，因为如果他们喜欢你，这就有帮助。它帮你把事情办成。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: The general story of make the gatekeepers happy and like you is true. I do think there are ways to overdo that for what it's worth. It becomes almost too transactional. If you show up with flowers for the EA, you better be damn confident in what you're doing, if that makes sense. But just like the small things go a long way. (00:52:50): You just make eye contact with them, thank them, respect them. If they bring you a coffee cup, ask them where to put it when you're done. Don't treat people who you might feel like the team or the staff feel that way, make them feel like part of the team it equals.
turns.zh: 让守门人开心、喜欢你，这个大道理是真的。但我确实觉得，就它的价值而言，有方式会做过头。它会变得几乎太功利。如果你带着花去见 EA，你最好对你做的事有十足把握，如果这说得通的话。但就像那些小事，作用长远。（00:52:50）：你只要和他们有眼神接触、谢谢他们、尊重他们。如果他们给你拿了咖啡杯，喝完问他们该放哪儿。别把你可能觉得是团队或员工的人那样对待，要让他们感觉像是团队的一份子，那才平等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The Calendly stuff, I feel like that's its own separate book of Calendly Etiquette.
turns.zh: Calendly 这事儿，我觉得它自己都能单独出一本《Calendly 礼仪》了。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Calendly is one of my favorite episodes of going hyperviral on something hilarious.
turns.zh: Calendly 是我最爱的话题之一——就某件好笑的事疯传全网这件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So one thing that Calendly does is you can embed. I don't do this yet, but I should. It feels like just embedding your times in the email feels like a good-
turns.zh: 那么 Calendly 做的一件事是你可以嵌入。我还没这么做，但我该这么做。感觉把你的时间直接嵌进邮件里，是个不错的——

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Look, I'll be honest, I go the other way. I don't use any of that stuff. And look, I think scheduling is very complicated. This is part of it. I always think of these, it's like, when are you free? It totally depends on who's asking. If Barack Obama, or I don't know, I won't say Donald Trump, someone wants to meet with me and it's like 4:00 in the morning my time, or I'm totally, "You know what? I'm going to make it work." (00:53:55): And so I do think I'm actually kind of against the flat hierarchy, all meetings are the same, da-da-da-da. That does mean, honestly, I think that you probably knocked me. My bet is that my calendar moves more than most people's, and I'm sure that feels disrespectful to some, and it is. I want to be really clear, but it's also the reality of trying to balance these things.
turns.zh: 看，我老实说，我走的是另一条路。我那些东西一个都不用。而且看，我觉得排日程非常复杂。这是其中一部分。我总是这么想这些事：你什么时候有空？这完全取决于谁在问。如果是 Barack Obama，或者我不知道——我不提 Donald Trump 了——某人想见我，哪怕是我这边的凌晨 4 点，我也会想：『你懂什么？我这就去把它安排成。』（00:53:55）：所以我确实有点反对那种扁平位阶、所有会议都一样的论调，吧啦吧啦。这确实意味着，老实说，我觉得你大概被我冒犯过。我打赌我的日历比大多数人的都动得勤，而且我确信这对某些人来说感觉不尊重，也确实如此。我想说得很清楚，但这同时也是试图平衡这些事的现实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other flaw with Calendly, I've realized someone once figured out my Calendly URL and just booked a meeting with me, like a founder wanting to pitch me, and it was on my calendar. I'm like, "Who is that?"
turns.zh: Calendly 的另一个漏洞是，我意识到有人曾经破解了我的 Calendly 链接，直接给我约了个会——就像一个想向我 pitch 的创始人——而它就出现在我日历上。我就想：『那是谁？』

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: The funny one I've had is there are people whose names are very similar to other people I know. And every once in a while, I've ended up accepting a cold meeting and showing up and be like, "You are not the person I expected." Because I was like, "Oh, your name is off by one letter." That's cool. That's not a thing to call out, by the way, from an etiquette perspective. Once you're committed to the meeting, you're doing the meeting, even if it's the wrong person.
turns.zh: 我遇到过好笑的是：有些人的名字和我认识的另一些人非常像。偶尔，我到最后接受了一个 cold meeting、然后到场才发现：『你不是我预期的那个。』因为我会想：『哦，你名字就差一个字母。』那挺酷的。顺便说，从礼仪角度，那不是该指出来的事。一旦你答应了这场会、你就在开这场会了，哪怕对方是错的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. Okay. Well, one last question with Calendly. Something I try to do, curious to get your take is like, okay, someone want a founder, I'm meeting with a founder and the way I approach it is like, okay, do you have a Calendly or something I could use to book a meeting with you? If not, in parentheses, here's my calendar in case that might make it easier.
turns.zh: 哦，天。好。那么关于 Calendly 最后一个问题。我试着在做的一件事，好奇你的看法：比如，有人——一个创始人——我想和一位创始人见面，我处理的方式是：好吧，你有 Calendly 或者我能用来跟你约会的什么吗？如果没有，括号里附上我的日历，以防那样能更方便些。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's perfectly fine in terms of the way to do it. I just think the key is to make it easy for the person you're trying to do business with.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得就做法而言完全没问题。我只是觉得关键是：让你想做生意的那个人省心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And not make them feel like they have to do the work if they don't want to.
turns.zh: 而且别让他们觉得，如果他们不想，就非得他们来费这个劲。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: No, you do the work. Basically, you're asking for something, you do the work is the upshot.
turns.zh: 不，你才该费劲。基本上，你在请求什么东西，你才该费劲——这就是要义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, sweet. Moving on to the next topic, communication.
turns.zh: 好，棒。进入下一个话题：沟通。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Don't use emojis, try to proofread your stuff, get to the point quickly, assume the person you're reading is busy. Again, I think these are all the types of things that none of this is rocket science from my perspective, but people, it's just good to remember and be on top of it. I do think people have different things on this. I personally do think that on things like email, you kind of do have an SLA to respond. (00:55:53): There's some people I know who are like, "Email does not mean I have to respond. You send me an email, you may or may not get a response. It's completely up to me. I have no contract to respond to your email." I personally go the other way, which I feel like from an etiquette perspective, I don't owe you a 12-page essay, but I do owe at least an acknowledgement quickly of what you've sent. (00:56:13): You don't want to leave people hanging. But again, I just think it's like if you read an email, I'm sorry, if you write an email, imagine you're receiving it. How does it feel? Does it feel like you're asking a ton of the person you send it to? If you send them 10 paragraphs, it's annoying. You're like, "Okay, I have to read all this. What am I going to find time?" (00:56:33): This is like you're asking a lot. It's kind of like a monologue and a conversation. You've just said, "I'm going to spend 10 minutes talking at you." And so I do think keeping it short and to the point, not being silly, not using emoji, trying to make it readable. These are all important things.
turns.zh: 别用 emoji，尽量校对你的东西，快速切中要点，假设读的人很忙。再说一次，我觉得这些全都不是什么火箭科学——在我看来——但人们，记住并掌握好这些，就是好事。我确实觉得人们在这事上各有各的做法。就我个人而言，我觉得像是邮件这种，你多少有个回复的 SLA。（00:55:53）：我认识一些人会说：『邮件不代表我必须回。你给我发邮件，你可能收到回、也可能收不到。完全看我。我和你的邮件之间没有回复契约。』我个人走相反的路，我觉得从礼仪角度，我不欠你一篇 12 页的论文，但我确实欠你一个对你所发内容的快速确认。（00:56:13）：你不想让人悬着。但再说一次，我就觉得，如果你读一封邮件——抱歉，如果你写一封邮件——想象你收到它。感觉如何？它让人觉得你在向收件人索取一大堆吗？如果你发过去十个段落，那很烦人。你会想：『好，我得把这些都读完。我哪找时间？』（00:56:33）：这就像你在索取很多。它有点像对话里的独白。你刚说了：『我要花 10 分钟对着你讲。』所以我确实觉得，保持简短、切中要点，别犯傻、别用 emoji、尽量让它易读。这些全都是重要的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say more about the emoji piece. Is your advice just know emojis if it's a business?
turns.zh: 多说一点 emoji 这块。你的建议只是说：如果是公事，就别用 emoji 吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I think emoji from my perspective, it's quite a step of familiarity, if that makes sense. From a business context, look, if someone sends you a smiley face, you can respond with it. You can kind of match. Again, it goes back to this matching vocabulary and language. I'm not saying you should be totally cut and dry, but it's kind of, I would say emojis almost feel like jokes to me, which is like, tell them at your own risk and they're probably not worth it.
turns.zh: 我觉得 emoji，从我的角度，是相当大的一步亲昵——如果这说得通的话。在商务语境里，看，如果有人给你发了个笑脸，你可以回一个。你可以稍微匹配。再说一次，这回到匹配词汇和语言上。我不是说你该完全干巴巴，但我会说，emoji 在我这儿几乎感觉像笑话——也就是，讲不讲随你冒险，而且它们大概不值得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. I do use emojis. I use the thank you hands one a lot.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好。我确实用 emoji。我老用那个双手合十感谢的。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Look, I think text is different. I think people might have slightly different takes on this. And so I wouldn't say anything I'm saying here is dogmatic, but I'm just saying that, again, emojis are not highly legible to most people. They can mean lots of different things. (00:57:39): They usually have cultural connotation to them. And I would say that they're kind of harder to read than just a well-worded, simple to the point email, and I think you just want to come across as a literate to the point, simple, clear person.
turns.zh: 看，我觉得文字消息不一样。我觉得人们在这事上看法可能略有不同。所以我不会说我说的话里有任何教条，但我只是说，再说一次，emoji 对大多数人来说并不是高度易读的。它们可以表示很多不同的意思。（00:57:39）：它们通常带文化含义。而我会说，它们比一封措辞得当、简单切题的邮件更难读懂，而我觉得你只想让人觉得你是个有文化、切题、简单、清楚的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And emoji sometimes kind of implies used AI to generate this thing because ChatGPT loves emojis.
turns.zh: 而且 emoji 有时有点暗示这东西是用 AI 生成的，因为 ChatGPT 爱用 emoji。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Totally. And I also say, look, there's a whole ... We want to get spicy for a second.
turns.zh: 完全对。而且我还要说，看，有整个……我们想稍微来点刺激的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I don't know how I feel about people who have invested too much in their emojis. So you get people who have changed the colors of their emojis from the default or whatever. I'm not saying not to do it. I'm just saying it's quite a statement is my view that you've invested in your emoji pack or using special emojis people haven't seen before or it's like, again, it's a subtlety and you got to understand the room and the culture and what you're responding to, but I do think that people read more into that than people want to be read into it.
turns.zh: 我不知道我对那些在自己的 emoji 上投入太多的人是什么感觉。所以你会遇到那些把自己 emoji 的颜色从默认改掉之类的。我不是说别那么做。我只是说，我的看法是，你投入了你的 emoji 包、或者用了别人从没见过 special emoji，那相当是一种表态——就像，再说一次，这是个微妙处，你得看懂这个房间、这种文化、以及你在回应什么，但我确实觉得，人们对那读出东西，比人们想被读出的要多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You know what's crazy now? I don't know if you've seen this, you can create your own emojis now in iOS and emojis are so ... It's like a whole new world, just infinite emojis.
turns.zh: 你知道现在多疯吗？我不知道你有没有看到，现在在 iOS 里你能创建自己的 emoji 了，而 emoji 这么……就像一整个新世界，无穷无尽的 emoji。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: But again, it's like if you choose to use those, you are going way out on a limb that people are going to be receptive to that and not be like, "This is a person who spent a lot of their time customizing their emoji pack when they probably should be doing something more interesting."
turns.zh: 但再说一次，这就像，如果你选择用那些，你是在大冒险——人们会接纳它，而不是像：『这是个把自己大把时间花在定制 emoji 包上、而本该去做点更有趣之事的人。』

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They should be finding product market fit.
turns.zh: 他们本该去寻找产品市场契合。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, or learning etiquette.
turns.zh: 对，或者去学礼仪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other tip you had that I loved, which is think about the order of the emails when you're emailing somebody.
turns.zh: 你另一条我超爱的建议是：发邮件时，想想收件人和抄送的顺序。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, I do think you kind of want to think about ... There is a connotation to who you send it to and who you CC and the order in which people. Now, I don't want to overstate this, but put differently, it's like if you're sending an email and the first person on the email is the assistant and the fourth person on the email is the CEO, you've probably done it wrong.
turns.zh: 对，我确实觉得你多少该想想……你发给谁、抄送谁、以及人们的顺序，是有含义的。现在，我不想夸大这点，但换个说法：如果你发一封邮件，邮件上第一个人是助理、第四个人是 CEO，那你可能搞错了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And because the implication there is who you think is most important comes first. Who's first to mind?
turns.zh: 因为那里的隐含意思是：你觉得最重要的人排在最前。谁最先浮上心头？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Well, who are you really sending this to? You know what I mean? It's almost the way I think and who's kind of included. So if I look at an email and I'm the first person in the two, candidly, I mildly pay more attention to it than when I'm the fifth, right? Because in my head I'm like, "Okay, well, this is really to Kevin and I'm on it." (00:59:53): If you see an email sent to many, many, many people, almost by definition, it's not that important is almost the way I would put And so you have to be really careful with managing that. I think even the who do you send it to and who do you CC. There's a language to that from an etiquette perspective to understand. And I do think people sometimes miss that. The CC line is very, very valuable. (01:00:13): It means, "Hey, you should have a copy of this. This is not really to you. I'm not expecting an immediate response." I even think there's even a subtlety who responds then. If you send an email to 10 people CC'd to the whole nine yards, there is a subtle etiquette to when you respond. (01:00:30): If you are the fifth CC on an email, you're not expected to be the first response. Again, you can break this rule. There are times to break it. There's a subtlety to it, but it wasn't really sent to you. And so there's a whole language to who you send to and who you CC in the order that, again, it's very subtle, but is worth understanding.
turns.zh: 嗯，你这封邮件到底真正发给谁？你懂我意思吧？这差不多是我思考的方式，以及谁被含进去了。所以如果我看到一封邮件，而我列在前两个人里，坦白讲，我比当我列在第五个时会稍微多留意一点，对吧？因为我脑子里会想：『好，嗯，这其实是要给 Kevin 的，我只是抄上。』（00:59:53）：如果你看到一封发给很多、很多、很多人的邮件，几乎按定义，它就没那么重要——差不多我会这么讲。所以你得非常小心地管理这个。我觉得，就连你发给谁、抄送谁，从礼仪角度都有一套语言值得理解。而我确实觉得人们有时漏掉了这点。抄送（CC）那一行非常、非常有价值的。（01:00:13）：它的意思是：『嘿，你该留一份副本。这其实不是发给你的。我不期待你立刻回。』我甚至觉得，连谁来回都是个微妙处。如果你发一封邮件给 10 个人、并把所有人 CC 到底，那在何时回复上就有微妙的礼仪。（01:00:30）：如果你是邮件上第五个被 CC 的人，没人期待你第一个回。再说一次，你可以打破这条规则。有打破的时机。这里有微妙处，但它本来就不是真发给你的。所以关于你发给谁、抄送谁、以及以什么顺序，有一整套语言——再说一次，它很微妙，但值得理解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So true. Man, and you would think nobody sees all these little things in the Gmail thread, but you do. They're just right there and you're like-
turns.zh: 太对了。天，你会以为没人在 Gmail 会话里注意到这些小细节，但你确实会。它们就明摆在眼前，然后你就——

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: This is the whole thing about etiquette is it's all this invisible stuff that you don't need to spend all ... In some ways, the whole story of doing this well is it should not occupy 80% of your brain. What you're saying is, "I've got this. We're on the same wavelength. My heart rate is low. I'm doing it properly and I'm doing it with intuitively almost." Which is a hard ask because what we're basically saying is these are unknown things, but intuitively you should just know them. And that is actually what you're signaling is you can trust me because intuitively, there's this well of knowledge and cultural connection and whatever that we can share effectively.
turns.zh: 这就是关于礼仪的全部：它全都是这些看不见的东西，你不需要把全部精力……在某种程度上，做好这件事的全部故事是：它不该占据你大脑的 80%。你表达的是：『这我搞得定。我们在同一波长。我心率低。我做对了，而且几乎是凭直觉在做。』这是个很高的要求，因为我们基本上是在说：这些是不成文的规矩，但直觉上你本就该知道它们。而那其实正是你在发出的信号——你可以信任我，因为直觉上，有一口知识和文化连接的水井，我们能有效地共享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And if your BCC definitely do not reply all.
turns.zh: 而且如果你被密送（BCC），绝对别回复全部。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah. I have some unbelievably funny faux pas from my history with CC/BCC To lines. One of the worst etiquette/mistakes I ever made, never, ever, ever put someone you're talking about who's not on an email in the To line to check the spelling of their name and then hit send. That's a bad idea. So whatever you're doing, that's not even an etiquette thing. That's just being smart.
turns.zh: 对。我在 To 行、CC/BCC 上犯过一些难以置信地好笑的失礼。我犯过最糟糕的礼仪错误之一：永远、永远、永远别把你在聊的、但没在邮件里的人，放进 To 行去核对他名字的拼写，然后点发送。那是个馊主意。所以无论你在做什么，那甚至都不算礼仪问题。那只是聪明点而已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Proofreading thing.
turns.zh: 校对那件事。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Proofread. Proofread. And don't send emails to people about them that they're not supposed to see.
turns.zh: 校对。校对。而且别发那种本不该被对方看到的、关于他们的邮件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's like Gmail makes it too easy to do that because it adds them automatically if you have their name.
turns.zh: 而且 Gmail 让这太容易发生了，因为如果你有他们的名字，它会自动把人加进去。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: No, for me it was more just like the way to check the spelling of someone's name is not to put them in the To field, ever.
turns.zh: 不，对我来说，更多的是：核对某人名字拼写的方式，绝不是把他们放进 To 栏——永远别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. Oh man. Well, you're still kicking, so it wasn't so bad.
turns.zh: 对。好。哦天。嗯，你还活蹦乱跳的，所以也没那么糟。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I'm still kicking.
turns.zh: 我还活蹦乱跳。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. Okay. Two more. Meeting etiquette.
turns.zh: 好，棒。好。还有两个。会议礼仪。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah. Again, we've talked about arriving a little bit early. You should do that. Don't arrive up too, too early. Again, if you're an hour early, walk around the block. It's fine to walk around the block. You don't want to sit in someone's office, because then all of a sudden it feels like this person's been here a long time. (01:02:49): It feels like even though they're not scheduled, we're leaving them hanging. You're six coffees deep with the receptionist. You don't want that. So I think you want to be 10 to 15 minutes early. You do not want to be much earlier than that. We talked about meeting other convenience. I do think it's fine to start with a little bit of small talk. (01:03:10): There are times it's not or times people are running behind, but the pleasantry of the weather is nice or how is your weekend? Or something that kind of cuts the air a little bit and then you flip into business is a good thing. Even though it feels transparent, it's still useful is what I would say. And again, it's almost a signal of, I am here for business, but I am a normal person and I'm willing to have signaling like, "Oh, I know that we should start with a normal conversation." If that makes sense.
turns.zh: 对。再说一次，我们聊过稍微早到一点。你该这么做。别到得太、太早。再说一次，如果你早到一个小时，去街区绕一圈。绕街区走走没问题。你不想坐在别人的办公室里，因为那样突然间就会让人觉得这人已经在这儿很久了。（01:02:49）：它让人觉得，哪怕他们没被列入日程，我们也在让他们干等。你都已经和前台喝了六杯咖啡了。你不想那样。所以我觉得你想早到 10 到 15 分钟。你不该比那早太多。我们聊过会议的其他便利。我确实觉得以一点点寒暄开场没问题。（01:03:10）：有些时候不行，或者有时别人在后面赶，但聊聊天气这种客套、或者你周末怎么样？或者某种稍微破一下冰、然后你切回正事，是件好事。哪怕它感觉明显，它仍然有用——这是我想说的。再说一次，它差不多是个信号：我是来谈事的，但我也是个正常人，而且我愿意发出这种信号：『哦，我知道我们该从一段正常的对话开始。』如果这说得通的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if you saw this on Twitter. Someone described small talk as the TCP/IP act handshake.
turns.zh: 我不知道你有没有在 Twitter 上看到。有人把寒暄描述为 TCP/IP 的三次握手。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I love it. It's a great description. I always describe it as like, imagine the modem crash from when we were kids on a 424. That old modem crash. That's what small talk is. It's a modem crash. We're trying to hit the wavelengths, et cetera, is the way-
turns.zh: 我爱这个。这描述太棒了。我总把它描述成：想象我们小时候用 424 上网时那个调制解调器的啸叫。那老式的调制解调器啸叫。那就是寒暄。它是一次调制解调器啸叫。我们在试着对上波长，之类——差不多是这么个——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so that you're ready to talk, so they ready to really communicate.
turns.zh: 于是你就准备好说话了，于是他们也就准备好真正沟通了。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah. For meetings, virtual ones, camera on. And again, I say this as someone who sometimes violates this. I violate it knowingly. I violate it knowing what it costs me, but you really should have your camera on. And again, you should dress appropriately for a video call. You should have an appropriate background. If you have your bed in your background, it should be nicely made. You know what I mean? (01:04:28): In some ways it's like doing the easy stuff is the key. And I go a step further. I actually, this is less a hard rule. I actually really don't love virtual backgrounds for the same reason. I'm like, "Look, I'm not going to judge you if you're in your bedroom, if you're a startup founder. It's fine, but I would like to see that your bed is made." Or I'll give you another one that's classic that I see with founders all the time. (01:04:55): Close your closet. People will get on Zoom calls and you'll be on a call and their closet is open and I'm like, "It's not a big deal, but do you see your own self picture here? Can you just close your closet? I don't want to see your shirts." That type of stuff I think goes further than people realize.
turns.zh: 对。会议，虚拟的那类，开摄像头。再说一次，我这么说，是作为一个有时违反这条的人。我有意识地违反它。我明知代价仍违反它，但你真的该开着摄像头。再说一次，你该为视频通话穿得得体。你该有个得体的背景。如果你背景里有床，它该铺得整整齐齐。你懂我意思吧？（01:04:28）：在某种程度上，把那些容易的事做了，就是关键。而且我还要更进一步。其实，这不太算硬性规则。其实我真的很不喜欢虚拟背景，原因相同。我会想：『看，如果你是创业公司创始人，在你卧室里，我不会评判你。那没事，但我希望能看到你的床铺好了。』或者再给你一个我老在创始人身上看到的经典款。（01:04:55）：关上你的衣柜。人们会登上 Zoom 通话，而你正通着话，他们的衣柜开着，我就想：『这倒不是大事，但你看得到你自己这儿的画面吗？你就不能关上衣柜吗？我不想看到你的衬衫。』这类事，我觉得比人们意识到的更深远。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. One other tip you had was clean up after yourself if you're in a real meeting.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你还有一条建议是：如果你在真实会议里，要自己收拾。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: The easiest way, and this is by the way, it's for my partner, Kevin Colleran, But the easiest way to come off badly is to not offer to put your coffee cup in the kitchen. And honestly, we do this because if you think about it, we work for LPs, limited partners. That's who we raise money from and then deploy it from. (01:05:40): And my partner, Kevin, even more than me, has this thing, which is he is maniacal about this, which is no matter who's in the room, if we're with an LP, you take the coffee, you take the Diet Coke. Even if you know full well, someone's going to come in and clean up after you and you make a point of asking where we can put it or putting it on the side table, et cetera, and acknowledging that there is a mess.
turns.zh: 最简单的办法——而且顺带说，这是我合伙人 Kevin Colleran 的——最容易让人印象差的方式，就是不去主动把你的咖啡杯放进厨房。而且老实说，我们这么做，是因为你想想就知道：我们为 LPs（有限合伙人）工作。那就是我们募资、然后部署资金的对象。（01:05:40）：而我合伙人 Kevin，甚至比我还执着于这事，他会为这个发疯——无论房间里是谁，如果是和一位 LP 在一起，你拿走咖啡、你拿走健怡可乐。哪怕你完全清楚会有人进来帮你收拾，你也要特意问我们该放哪儿、或者把它放到边桌上等等，并且承认这里有一摊乱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel that. Final topic is exiting and leaving. What are some tips?
turns.zh: 我懂这个。最后一个话题是退场和离开。有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: You should stand where people leave the table, right? Not ridiculously. By the way, you should go stand with the table. Stand to shake hands. Don't be sitting when you're shaking your hands. It's just what you do. And it shows that you're aware of it. (01:06:16): Follow up with gratitude. You should send people thank you notes. They shouldn't be long. They shouldn't be ridiculous, but we met. I got something out of it. Thank you for taking your time is always appreciated is what I would say. Obviously there's stuff like don't take calls, et cetera. This is the kind of obvious stuff in terms of exiting and how you think about it. (01:06:40): Even if someone rings you and the meeting's over and you're overtime, you're like, "I got to pick up this call." You hit the button that says I'm calling you right back and then walk away. Don't just pick up the phone and wave, is what I would say. Yeah, and I think there's stuff like that that I would just keep in mind.
turns.zh: 你该在人们离桌的地方站起来，对吧？别夸张。顺便说，你该去和桌子一起站着。站着握手。握手的时候别坐着。那就是你该做的。而且它表明你意识到了。（01:06:16）：事后带着感激跟进。你该给人发感谢信。它们不该长。它们不该荒唐，但我们见过面。我有所收获。谢谢你拨冗——这永远会被感激，这是我想说的。显然还有诸如别接电话之类的事。就退场、以及你怎么看待它而言，这是那种显而易见的东西。（01:06:40）：哪怕有人打电话给你、会议已结束、你已超时，你心想：『我得接这个电话。』你按那个我马上打回给你的键，然后走开。别就直接拿起电话挥一挥，这是我想说的。对，我觉得这类事我就记在心里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also, don't make a production if you're exiting, just exit.
turns.zh: 还有，如果你在退场，别搞得像演一出戏，直接走就是。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yes, I think that's really true. There's even a point to like, there are lots of scenarios where I think an Irish goodbye is the best goodbye where you just kind of disappear. Any large group setting I think is great. Maybe you thank one person on the way out of the host. But the I am leaving now, right? Let me kind of say goodbye to everyone and hug everyone. It's too much. It's too much.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得那真的对。甚至有个点是：有很多场景里，我觉得爱尔兰式告别是最好的告别——你就那么消失掉。任何大群聚的场合，我觉得都适用。也许你在出去路上谢一个人、也就是东道主。但那种我现在要走了，对吧？让我跟每个人道个别、跟每个人抱一下，太过了。太过了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Okay. We got through everything. Is there anything else that you think might be important to share?
turns.zh: 我爱这个。好。我们过完所有了。你还有什么觉得重要、该分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: There's so much other stuff. Again, I go back to this whole thing, which is like, these are all fun tips. I love the cartoons. We iterated them a bunch. We have more to do. We're having a lot of fun with this and I think it is providing a lot of value to people, which is great. That's kind of my goal is to both have fun and actually provide value and help people. That intersection is great. (01:07:49): There's a thousand other tips. And so for the biggest thing for me is when you have more or think of them, send them to us because there'll be a second version of the book and then a third. And I actually really want to cite the people who contribute to it. The book is what? 50, 60 pages. It will be a few hundred eventually. And I think there's a lot more to come and we're going to be doing classes next year all over the country and actually world. We're going to do one in Tel Aviv.
turns.zh: 还有太多别的东西。再说一次，我回到这整件事，它差不多是：这些都是好玩的建议。我爱那些漫画。我们反复打磨了它们好几轮。我们还有更多要做。我们玩得很开心，而且我觉得它给人们提供了很多价值，这很棒。我的目标差不多就是：既好玩，又真正提供价值、帮助人们。那个交集很棒。（01:07:49）：还有一千条别的建议。所以对我来说最重要的一点是：当你有更多、或者想到它们时，发给我们，因为这本书会有第二版、然后第三版。而且我真的想标注那些贡献的人。这本书现在多少页？50、60 页。最终会变成几百页。而且我觉得还有更多会来，我们明年会在全国、其实全世界开课。我们会在特拉维夫开一场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: We're going to do one. We're certainly doing one in New York and a few other places and it'll be fun.
turns.zh: 我们会开一场。我们肯定会在纽约、以及其他几个地方开，而且会很好玩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God. You got a whole new life forming here.
turns.zh: 我的天。你这儿正长出一整个新人生。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: The funny thing is this stuff, the etiquette story is obviously pretty fun. And so people like Morning Brew just keep making videos about this and there's this whole etiquette thing going on. And I'm like, "Oh my God, I've done some pretty good investments in my life, built some cool products. Am I going to be ultimately remembered as the etiquette guy? That's kind of hilarious."
turns.zh: 好笑的是，这事儿——礼仪这个故事——显然挺好玩的。所以像 Morning Brew 这种机构就一直做关于它的视频，整个礼仪热潮在进行。而我就想：『我的天，我这辈子做过一些相当不错的投资、造过一些很酷的产品。我最终会不会就因为礼仪先生而被记住？那可真有点滑稽。』

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what we're doing here.
turns.zh: 那正是我们在这儿做的事。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I'm into it though. I'm into it. I'm fine with that.
turns.zh: 不过我挺投入的。我挺投入的。我对此没意见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you have the TLDR at the beginning. I'll just read this real quick and add anything that we're missing.
turns.zh: 所以你在开头有个 TLDR。我就快速读一下，再补点我们漏掉的。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, sure.
turns.zh: 对，当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this is just like what to do if you do nothing else. Remember the goal of all etiquette is essentially building trust and project genuine confidence. Always maintain an abundance mindset. Remember that you are worthy and have nothing to prove and that it's okay to ask questions and keep your heart rate low.
turns.zh: 所以这就像是：如果你别的都不做，该做什么。记住，所有礼仪的目标，本质上是建立信任、并展现出真实的自信。始终保持丰盈心态。记住你是有价值的、没什么需要证明的，而且提问没问题、保持低心率没问题。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: That's the points. If nothing else, if you remember those points, we will be served well.
turns.zh: 那就是那些要点。如果别的都不记，只要你记住那些点，我们就受益匪浅了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There we go. Okay. I'm going to take us to close out and make this more of a regular episode. I'm going to take us to two recurring segments on the podcast, AI corner and Contrarian corner. I don't know if I told you I was going to ask you these questions, but I'm going to go for it.
turns.zh: 这就对了。好。我要带我们收个尾，让这期更像一期常规节目。我要带我们进入播客里两个固定的环节：AI 角和逆向角。我不知道有没有跟你说我要问你这些问题，但我这就来。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: You lay it on me. I love Contrarian corner. An AI corner depends what you mean by that.
turns.zh: 你尽管问。我爱逆向角。AI 角嘛，得看你指的是什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the question in AI corner is just what's one way you've found AI useful in your worker life that might be helpful for people to hear?
turns.zh: 那么 AI 角的问题是：你在工作生活里发现 AI 有什么用处，可能值得一提、对大家有帮助的？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: So look, I'm by default pretty skeptical of most AI applications. I will say the thing that I've had the most fun with with AI and I find great is it actually is partially where the cartoons for this came from is I built a little personal news aggregator called Letter Meme that basically takes all the newsletters I don't have time to read and turns them into daily cartoons. (01:09:56): So I have a grid of what's going on in the world as a front page in cartoons. And I actually love it. It's like the best way I get an overview because there's all these smart newsletters, you don't have time to read any of them. So I piped them all in and-
turns.zh: 看，我默认对大多数 AI 应用都相当怀疑。我要说，我和 AI 玩得最开心、也觉得最棒的事——其实部分上，这书的漫画就是从那儿来的——是我做了一个小个人新闻聚合器，叫 Letter Meme，它基本把我没时间读的所有通讯，变成每天的漫画。（01:09:56）：所以我有一格一格的、用漫画呈现的世界上在发生什么，像是个头版。而我是真爱它。那差不多是我获取概览最好的方式，因为有所有这些聪明的通讯，你却没时间读任何一篇。所以我把它们全接了进去，然后——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Except Lenny's Newsletter, but keep going.
turns.zh: 除了 Lenny 的通讯，不过继续。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: And what? Except Lenny's Newsletter. Sure, of course. That one I don't put in the aggregator, although of course I don't do that, but it's great. So I'm super into it.
turns.zh: 什么？除了 Lenny 的通讯。当然，那当然。那本我没放进聚合器，虽然当然我不会那么做，但它很棒。所以我超级投入。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's lettermeme.com. I'm checking it out. I love this. So this is AI generated, aggregates all the important newsletters and creates a little summary and a cartoon.
turns.zh: 那是 lettermeme.com。我在看。我爱这个。所以这是 AI 生成的，聚合所有重要的通讯，生成一个小摘要和一幅漫画。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, and you can make your own. So for me, I actually, I'm looking at this now, there's actually one thing that got messed up on this we need to change. But yeah, the idea is you basically get an email digest once a day and it's continuously updated to what's going on in the world and you pipe your own newsletters into it. So it's like whatever you actually trust and pay attention to.
turns.zh: 对，而且你可以做自己的。所以对我来说，我现在正看着这个，其实有一样东西搞错了、我们需要改。但对，想法是：你基本每天收到一封邮件摘要，它会持续更新成世界上正在发生的事，而你可以把自己的通讯接进去。所以它就像是你真正信任、真正留意的那些东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Genius. And how did you build this? Was it vibe coded? Did you have an engineer help you?
turns.zh: 天才。那你是怎么造出来的？是 vibe coding 出来的吗？还是有工程师帮你？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Well, both actually. I actually, the vibe coding thing, this is exactly what vibe coding is good for is like, this is like cursor and digital ocean and Cloudflare will get you a long way in terms of just building this stuff on the fly. And so I built the first version of this myself end to end, but then vibe coding also doesn't really scale. And so the reality is after a certain point, I had some friends who are great engineers just take it and up level in a few ways that I honestly ran out of time to work on.
turns.zh: 嗯，其实两者都有。其实，vibe coding 这事儿，它正好就是 vibe coding 擅长的：像这样，cursor 加 digital ocean 加 Cloudflare，在临时搭这种东西上能让你走很远。所以我从端到端自己造了第一版，但然后 vibe coding 也确实不能真扩展。所以现实是，过了某个点，我有些很厉害的工程师朋友就接手、把它在几个方面升级了——老实说，我自己已经没时间弄了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let's go to Contrarian corner. This could be an entire podcast conversation with you, I suspect, but just like what's something you want to share that you believe that most other people don't believe?
turns.zh: 好，我们进逆向角。我猜，这能跟你聊成一整期播客，但就简单说：有什么你相信、而大多数别人不相信的东西，你想分享？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I think that the venture capital, the seed venture capitalists who invest in companies that are branded as AI companies are going to lose an impossibly large amount of money in the coming years. And that doesn't mean that I don't think you should be using AI to build things. I actually think you absolutely should. (01:11:44): It's kind of like not using AI in your startup is the equivalent of not using the cloud in 2010 or not using the internet in 2000. It would be insane. Of course we're going to use these tools, but there's a difference between a great business that you're using AI to supercharge or make better or just as a piece of infrastructure. That's not an AI business. (01:12:03): This is a business and I'm very into those versus all of these companies that come out that say we are the AI blank, I think they're all going to zero. Even my kind of argument this from a seed perspective is like, look, is OpenAI a good investment or not? It's a terrible seed investment, right? The way the number's baked out, even at a $500 billion market cap when all said and done, the seed investors have made something like 25 times their money. That's insane if you think about it. That's basically the worst. (01:12:33): It's like a middling at best seed investment for the company that is defining the moment. And the reason is because these things are so capital consumptive. So if you're trying to deploy $100 billion, the market is fragmented, people want to dream a dream, people want religion, they want belief. There's a bunch of reasons why you can squint and justify it. You know what? If the storytelling of Elon allows SpaceX, which by the way, I love, I think SpaceX is an awesome company, but if all of a sudden that actually can be worth $1.4 trillion to the public market, guess what? (01:13:06): The money plowers are going to do great with all this narrative driven religion is what I would put it, but if you're a disciplined seed investor, I guess my contrary intake would be run away from things that are AI companies because even if you look smart for the moment, you're playing a dangerous game of get out before the narrative collapses.
turns.zh: 我觉得，风投——那些投被贴上 AI 公司标签的公司的种子轮风投——未来几年会亏掉一笔不可能大的钱。而这不代表我觉得你不该用 AI 去造东西。其实我觉得你绝对该用。（01:11:44）：它差不多就像：在你的创业公司里不用 AI，等同于 2010 年不用云、或者 2000 年不用互联网。那会疯掉。我们当然要用这些工具，但区别在于：你用 AI 来加速、或做得更好、或者只是当作一块基础设施——那不是一家 AI 公司。（01:12:03）：这是一家公司，我对此非常投入；相对地，所有那些出来说我们是 AI 某某的公司，我觉得它们全都会归零。就连我从种子轮角度的论点是：看，OpenAI 算不算好投资？它是糟糕透顶的种子轮投资，对吧？按那个数字算下来，哪怕最终 5000 亿美元市值，种子轮投资者也就赚了大约 25 倍。你想想，那很疯。那基本就是最糟的。（01:12:33）：对那家定义这个时刻的公司来说，这差不多只是中等偏下的种子轮回报。原因就是这些东西太吃资本了。所以如果你要部署 1000 亿美元，市场是碎片化的，人们想要做梦、想要宗教、想要信念。有一堆理由让你眯着眼就能合理化它。你知道吗？如果 Elon 的叙事能让 SpaceX——顺便说，我爱它，我觉得 SpaceX 是个超棒的公司——但万一它突然对公开市场真值 1.4 万亿美元，你猜怎么着？（01:13:06）：那些资金耕耘者，会靠着这种叙事驱动的信条大赚——这是我会下的判语；但如果你是个纪律严明的种子轮投资者，我猜我的逆向直……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I love this. Okay. I want to follow this through a little bit. So you're saying because of the dilution that goes along with these companies.
turns.zh: 哇。我爱这个。好。我想顺着这个稍微追一下。所以你是说，因为这些公司伴随而来的稀释。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's like they're too capital. If they work, they're too capital intensive. Seed investing does not work in highly capital intensive businesses, so that's not going to happen. Two, they're fundamentally commoditizing in all sorts of ways. It's very unclear what the lock-in or value is on any of these things. And so it's just like the whole dynamic is off, and the thing is people are desperate right now for things to believe in. (01:13:54): If you think about the history, we've done so well as a country with Terra Nova. The US was amazing for so many years because we had the West, and if you were going to work hard, you could go west and you'd do great. And there was all this opportunity, land of opportunity. We've had reverberated, my generation, your generation, we were blessed because we had the internet. The internet was digital Terra Nova and we got to build fortunes and do amazing stuff and new work be in this new world that was created, but it was effectively the same thing as the West all over again. (01:14:23): And ever since then, whether it's mobile, which again, if you look at the math on it, everyone wants it to be disruptive in Terra Nova, not really. It's just more internet or like crypto, which by the way, I think crypto is amazing. I think it's the closest thing to Terra Nova, but to now the AI God narratives, every generation is desperate for their Terra Nova story with good reason, right? But the story is it has to be real. And I think unfortunately this time, this is a classic example of AI is a powerful tool. It's incredibly powerful for existing businesses and existing structures. It's not a great startup opportunity.
turns.zh: 它就像它们太吃资本。如果它们成了，也太资本密集。种子轮投资在高度资本密集的生意里行不通，所以那不会发生。其二，它们在各种意义上根本性地被商品化了。这些玩意儿里，锁定效应或价值到底是什么，非常不清楚。所以整个动态就是错位了，而关键是，人们现在极度渴望有东西可以去信。（01:13:54）：你想想历史，我们作为一个国家，靠 Terra Nova（新大陆）过得那么好。美国那么多好年景，是因为我们有西部，而如果你肯努力，你可以往西走、并且大有所成。还有那么多机会，机会之地。我们这代、你们这代，都被眷顾了，因为我们有了互联网。互联网就是数字版的 Terra Nova，我们得以建造财富、做惊人的事、在这个被创造出来的新世界里从事新工作——但它其实和西部是同一回事，又来了一遍。（01:14:23）：从那以后，无论是移动——再说一次，你看它的账，人人都想要它在 Terra Nova 意义上是颠覆性的，其实并不是。它只是更多互联网；或者像 crypto，顺便说，我觉得 crypto 很惊人。我觉得它是最接近 Terra Nova 的东西；但直到现在的 AI 上帝叙事，每一代人都极度渴望属于自己的 Terra Nova 故事，这有充分理由，对吧？但故事是：它得是真的。而我觉得不幸的是，这一次，这是个经典的例子——AI 是个强大的工具。它对既有企业和既有结构来说无比强大。它不是一个好的创业机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what is it you look for? What do you look for when you're investing in AI startup?
turns.zh: 那你找的是什么？当你投 AI 创业公司时，你找的是什么？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Well, again, I won't invest anything that I would consider an AI startup. I'll invest in things that use AI. For me, I think I'm really interested in the cultural implications of AI or the new businesses that need to exist because it is a force in the world. So we've done a lot, whether it's Sublime Security or Outtake, things like that that are basically all around the theme of the Voight-Kampff test from Great Blade Runner, which was the test they used randomly, are you a real or are you a bot?
turns.zh: 嗯，再说一次，我不会投任何我会视为 AI 创业公司的东西。我会投那些用 AI 的东西。对我来说，我觉得我真正感兴趣的是 AI 的文化意涵，或者那些因为 AI 成为世界一股力量而需要存在的新生意。所以我们做了很多，无论是 Sublime Security 还是 Outtake，诸如此类，基本都围绕《银翼杀手》里 Voight-Kampff 测试这个主题——那个他们随机用的测试：你到底是真人，还是个机器人？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The turtle.
turns.zh: 那个乌龟。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: That's a huge problem.
turns.zh: 那是个大问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The turtle on their back?
turns.zh: 是它们背上那只乌龟？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah, so there's a whole set of companies that are implications of AI and how do you manage it and handle it as a society. I think there's a lot to do there. And there's a lot to do in cultural shifts from AI. There's all sorts of interesting trends to follow there. There's all sorts of businesses that will be disrupted. They're not AI businesses, they're businesses that'll be disrupted in interesting ways. (01:15:52): So I think there's a lot of opportunity, but again, I think there's a ... I at least draw a distinction between if you're trying to be ... certainly a foundation model company, but any of these things that are like, we're going to win because AI, I'm like, "No, you're going to win because of something else, and AI is going to be a propellant to it."
turns.zh: 对，所以有一整批公司，是 AI 的衍生影响——作为社会，我们该如何管理、处理它。我觉得那里有很多事可做。而且从 AI 带来的文化转变里，也有很多事可做。那里有各种有趣的潮流可循。有各种会被颠覆的生意。它们不是 AI 生意，它们是将以有趣方式被颠覆的生意。（01:15:52）：所以我觉得有很多机会，但再说一次，我觉得有个……我至少会做一个区分：如果你试图成为……当然是一家基础模型公司，但任何那种我们要靠 AI 赢的东西，我都会想：『不，你会赢，是因为别的什么，而 AI 会成为它的推进剂。』

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sam, you're a fascinating human. I feel like we could talk for hours. Is there anything before we get to our very exciting lightning round, anything else you wanted to share?
turns.zh: Sam，你是个迷人精。我觉得我们能聊上好几个小时。在我们进入超刺激的快问快答之前，还有什么你想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Look, I'm happy to be here. I love your work. It's good to be on your podcast. Happy to bullshit whenever. But no, we're good.
turns.zh: 看，我很高兴来这儿。我爱你的作品。能上你的播客真好。随时乐意瞎聊。但没了，我们挺好。

turns.en: Okay. Well, with that, we've reached a very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you.

turns.zh: 五个问题。我准备好了。

turns.zh: 五个问题。有哪两三本书，是你最常推荐给别人的？

turns.en: Ooh, okay. So let me pull up my list because I got to pull up my Kindle for this. One is I'm reading right now. I got to admit, I like to make fun of Marc Andreessen a lot, but he recommended a book called The Ancient City, which is fascinating. And so I'm in the middle of that right now. I'm really enjoying it. Man's Search for Meaning is great. I'm just going through. What have I read recently? You know what's great? (01:16:58): Area 51, An Uncensored History: The Top Secret Military Base. Not very Erudite, great book. And then I honestly think the one serious one I'll make a recommendation on is Lessons From History is one of my favorite books ever. I would really, really, really recommend it. It's a short read, but Lessons From History by Ariel Durant is probably the most approachable, non-obvious book I love.
turns.zh: 哦，好。让我调出我的清单，因为这我得翻出我的 Kindle。一本是我现在正读的。我得承认，我很爱拿 Marc Andreessen 开涮，但他推荐过一本叫《古代城市》的书，挺迷人的。所以我现在正读到一半。我真的很享受它。《活出意义来》很棒。我刚在过。我最近读了什么？你知道什么很棒吗？（01:16:58）：《51 区，一段未删节的历史：最高机密军事基地》。不算很有学问，但很棒的一本书。然后老实说，那本我会认真推荐的严肃之作是《历史的教训》，那是我有史以来最爱的书之一。我真的、真的、真的会推荐它。它很短，但 Ariel Durant 的《历史的教训》，大概是我最爱、最容易读、又不出所料的那种书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I did that one on Audible and you could just listen to it all in a couple hours.
turns.zh: 那本我是在 Audible 上听的，你几个小时就能全听完。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's a short read. It's not a long book. I honestly think for me-
turns.zh: 它很短。不是本长书。老实说我觉得对我——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A few hours.
turns.zh: 几个小时。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: ... Hours of investment to intellectual return. My one real answer right now would be that I could give you a thousand others from ... There are things like The Banana King. Have you heard this one? Have you seen this one?
turns.zh: ……几个小时的投入，换来智力上的回报。我现在唯一真正的答案是：我还能从……给你一千本别的。有像《香蕉之王》这种。你听过这个吗？你看过这个吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Oh my God, this is so good. What's it called? So The Fish that Ate the Whale. Incredible book. So is The Last Kings of Shanghai, if you know that one. These are all amazing books, but they're longer and there are more stories. Just everyone on the podcast should go read Will Durant.
turns.zh: 我的天，这太好了。它叫什么？是《吞下鲸鱼的鱼》。不可思议的一本书。还有《上海最后之王》，如果你知道那本的话。这些都是惊人的书，但它们更长、故事更多。播客上的各位就都去读 Will Durant 吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I love it. Favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 好。我爱这个。你最近真正享受的、最爱的电影或剧集是什么？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Oh, I got to say, recent, I think Landman is fabulous. Have you watched Landman?
turns.zh: 哦，我得说，最近的话，我觉得《兰德曼》太棒了。你看过《兰德曼》吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I've watched the latest episodes.
turns.zh: 看过。看过。我看了最新几集。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I'm really into it. That would be my most recent take.
turns.zh: 我超投入。那会是我最近的看法。

turns.en: What's interesting about that show is now tech companies are all super into energy and data centers.
turns.zh: 那部剧有意思的地方是：现在科技公司全都超级迷能源和数据中心。

turns.en: Well, I'll tell you a funny story, which I talked to a founder who's in Midland, Texas, which is kind of part of the show, and it's so classic and typical. He's like, all these Silicon Valley people and now think they understand the energy industry because they watched Landman. It's wild, but I totally believe it because I know too many venture capitalists are like, "Oh, I now understand this because I watched Landman." And he's like, "It's totally a thing."
turns.zh: 嗯，我给你讲个好笑的故事：我和一位在德州米德兰的创始人聊过，那地方差不多就是剧里的一部分，而那真经典、真典型。他会说：所有这些硅谷的人，现在都觉得他们懂能源行业了，就因为看了《兰德曼》。那很狂，但我完全信，因为我知道太多风投都像：『哦，我现在懂这个了，因为我看了《兰德曼》。』而他会说：『那完全是一回事。』

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I would feel that. Okay. Favorite product that you recently discovered that you love could be a gadget, could be an app, could be clothing.
turns.zh: 对，我也会有这感觉。好。你最近发现、并且超爱的产品是什么？可以是小工具、可以是应用、可以是衣服。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Okay, I'll pitch people on, this is a little self-serving, but I will pitch people on June date. So, okay, I actually don't use this product because I'm happily married, but this is cool. And here's the basic idea is if you think about so much of AI right now, this goes back to what businesses do you overhaul that are interesting that have AI implications, but are not AI. So everyone's got this whole virtual girlfriend, loneliness, you're going to chat with your friend, whatever, fine. These guys came out and what they do is they're like, look, if we're really trying to match up humans, call it Tinder 2.0, one of the best sources of information to do that is their ChatGPT histories. (01:19:42): So this app is kind of built around the premise of distilling, you ask ChatGPT a structured prompt that they've designed, it pulls out an unbelievably good profile of who you are and then you basically match with people based on what you're actually asking ChatGPT about and the implications of who you are and things like that. And the fun part is I haven't obviously done dates on it, not for me, but I have pulled my profile from like, "Wow, this is shockingly good description of who I actually am." And so I think that's a really fun business.
turns.zh: 好，我给人们安利一下，这有点自利，但我会给人们安利 June date。所以，嗯，其实我自己不用这产品，因为我婚姻幸福，但这很酷。基本想法是：你想想现在那么多 AI，这回到那个问题——有哪些有趣的、有 AI 意涵、却又不是 AI 的生意，你该去彻底改造？所以大家都有那一整套虚拟女友、孤独感、你要和你的朋友聊天之类的，行吧。这帮人冒出来，他们做的就像：看，如果我们真想撮合人类，管它叫 Tinder 2.0，那么做这件事最好的信息来源之一，就是他们的 ChatGPT 历史。（01:19:42）：所以这应用基本是围绕一个前提打造的：你向他们设计好的结构化提示问 ChatGPT，它会提炼出一个好得难以置信的、关于你是谁的画像，然后你基本就基于你实际在问 ChatGPT 的事、以及你是谁的意涵之类的，来和人匹配。好玩的部分是：我显然没在上面约过会——那不是给我用的——但我拉出过我自己的画像，像：『哇，这把我到底是谁描述得好得惊人。』所以我觉得那是门真好玩的生意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like that prompt that the ChatGPT folks once had of just visualize my space based on everything you know about me. And it was like, holy moly.
turns.zh: 那就像 ChatGPT 那帮人曾经有过的那个提示：就基于你对我的一切所知，把我的空间视觉化。然后就像，我的天。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's pretty good. It's pretty good.
turns.zh: 它挺好。它挺好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so in this dating app, I love this idea. It's so good. So do people read that? Are they able to see that as your profile or it's private?
turns.zh: 那么在这个交友应用里，我爱这个想法。太好了。所以人们会读那个吗？他们能把它当成你的资料看到，还是它是私密的？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: It's a little abstracted from that, but it's like the matching and the core thing is based on it. And again, I was just like, "Wow, this is good."
turns.zh: 它从那个稍微抽象出来一点，但匹配和核心的东西是基于它的。再说一次，我就想：『哇，这真好。』

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it goes on dates for you. Okay. So it simulates what a date might be like between you two potentially.
turns.zh: 而且它替你去约会。好。所以它模拟你们俩之间潜在的一场约会可能会是什么样。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: I guess.
turns.zh: 我猜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Your AI goes on dates for you, receives one high match, each one carefully. Wow, so fun.
turns.zh: 对。你的 AI 替你去约会，收到一个高匹配，每一个都精心安排。哇，太好玩了。

turns.en: It's good. I get it if you're single. I tried with my newsletter at one point, I was like, "Oh, honestly, the people who read my newsletter are pretty weird and specific." And so, "Hey, why don't I just offer a matchmaking service?" Where I'm like, "Okay, if you read my newsletter really and you're here, tell me who you are. I will build a little LLM and try to match with people." (01:21:11): Didn't work for me because candidly, you know what happened? Way too many qualified women and not enough men. I just don't have the liquidity. I have a hundred great women who wrote in being like, "Hey, this is what I'm looking for. This is who I am." And you're like, "You were an amazing person." And then the four guys who write in are like, "I want a 25-year-old hot girlfriend." This is not going to work, but June date might have the liquidity to make it
turns.zh: 它好。如果你是单身我懂。我有一度拿我的通讯试过，我就想：『哦，老实说，读我通讯的人挺怪、也挺特定的。』所以：『嘿，我干嘛不直接提供个撮合服务？』我就想：『好，如果你真读我的通讯、而且你在这儿，告诉我你是谁。我会搭个小 LLM，试着和人匹配。』（01:21:11）：对我没成，因为坦白讲，你猜发生了什么？太多够格的女性、却不够男性。我就是没有那个流动性。我有上百个很棒的女性写信进来，像：『嘿，这就是我在找的。这就是我。』然后你就想：『你是个了不起的人。』而那四个写进来的男生就像：『我要一个 25 岁的火辣女友。』这行不通，但 June date 也许有那个流动性，能把它做成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Work. By the way, your newsletter is awesome. Tell people where to find it while we're on that topic.
turns.zh: 做成。顺便说，你的通讯超棒。既然聊到这个话题，告诉大伙在哪儿能找到它。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: And I actually can't. There's no way to sign up for it. If you send me an email.
turns.zh: 而其实我没法说。没有注册它的途径。如果你给我发封邮件。

turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.en: If you send me an email lessin@gmail, I'm fine. Then if I respond, you get automatically added. I basically just, that's how people I'm interacting with get added, or I'll just add you. But it's actually funny. There's not ... Oh, you know you can do actually, I'll get you on it, is if you go to wlessin.com, I have my little bot app up that includes a little LLM that kind of is trained on my writing just because I was having fun building it. If you enter your email address there and talk to it, it will add you. But no, there's not like a signup page for it.
turns.zh: 如果你给我发邮件到 lessin@gmail，我没问题。然后如果我回，你就自动被加进去了。我基本就是——和我互动的人就那么被加进去，或者我直接加你。但这其实好笑。没有……哦，你知道你其实能——我会把你弄进去——如果你去 wlessin.com，我挂了个小机器人应用，里面有个小 LLM，大概是用我的写作训练的，就因为我在搭它时玩得开心。如果你在那儿输入邮箱、跟它聊，它就会加你。但不，它没有像个注册页那样的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I love this contrarian growth strategy. No, no, you can't really sign up. Okay, that's great. Okay, two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself coming back to often in work or in life?
turns.zh: 好。我爱这个逆向增长策略。不不，你其实没法注册。好，那太棒了。好，还有两个问题。你有没有一句最爱的、在工作和生活里常回到的生活格言？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: No, but I will say that I have hanging in my gym, which I love from the Facebook Hackathon after the launch of Google Plus. This is going way back in history. They made great posters, which was Carthage Must Burn. And it was just this great moment in work time when it was like, "Okay, game on, Google's coming for us." And I had some of the most fun work experiences. We were working literally 24 hours a day. Past midnight every night was in that period and I love that poster. So Carthage Must Burn. How about that?
turns.zh: 没有，但我会说，我健身房里挂着一句，我很爱它，出自 Google Plus 发布后那次 Facebook 黑客松。这要回溯到老早的历史了。他们做了超棒的海报，写着『迦太基必须焚毁』。那只是工作时段里一个超棒的瞬间，像：『好，开战了，Google 杀过来了。』而我有过一些最有趣的工作经历。我们那阵子 literally 一天干 24 小时。每个深夜都泡在那段日子里，而我爱那张海报。所以，迦太基必须焚毁。这个怎么样？

turns.en: Great. Final question. You are a fellow podcaster. I really enjoy your podcast called More or Less. It's very clever and lead named because of Lessin and with the Morins, Dave Morin.
turns.zh: 棒。最后一个问题。你也是个播客同行。我真的很享受你的播客《多或少》。它很聪明，之所以这么命名，是因为 Lessin、以及和 Morin 家的 Dave Morin。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: We love our lessons. My wife and I are contrarians and hate everything by default and the Morins think everything's amazing. So it kind of works from a dynamic perspective.
turns.zh: 我们爱我们的功课。我太太和我都是逆向派，默认憎恶一切，而 Morin 家觉得什么都惊人。所以从动态上讲，它差不多是成立的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love it. And Dave Morin and Brit Morin, just to be clear, and your wife, she runs the information.
turns.zh: 我会爱死它。而且说清楚，是 Dave Morin 和 Brit Morin，还有你太太，她经营着 The Information。

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: Yeah. So she's good at prompting us with it's actually going around the world and then we just bullshit about it.
turns.zh: 对。所以她很擅长给我们抛话题——其实它绕着全世界走一圈——然后我们就瞎聊一通。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what's something you've learned from that experience? I don't know. Any surprises about podcasting?
turns.zh: 那么从那个经历里，你学到了什么？我不知道。关于做播客，有什么意外吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Lessin
turns.en: So here's the thing, I think people ... It's kind of a weird podcast in some ways because honestly, I don't think any of us are highly filtered and it's kind of just like talking to your friends for an hour a week, which I want to do. I love the Morins. We don't live that close to them. (01:23:54): So it's kind of fun to just have that time set aside and then cut it up and post on the internet pretty raw. Here's the funny thing about it. It serves our purposes way more than I actually expected it to, which is we enjoy doing it, which is the most important part. We would do it if no one was listening. And weirdly, a lot of our friends and people we care about in the industry seem to pick up the pieces they like from it and talk to us about it. (01:24:19): And so it's like a great conversation starter. So it's like weird. It's not a huge podcast. It's big enough, but I actually think the thing that's been most surprising to me about it is that even though we don't really have growth strategies and we're not trying to blow it up and we don't get paid for it, it's like weirdly useful is what I would say. Even the fact that it's like ... I don't know. (01:24:41): I'm not sure if that's your experience too, and I think your podcast is probably much larger than ours, but it's weirdly listened to and useful by the people that we care about and it's fun despite the fact that it's not like a ... I don't know, it's not all in or something yet. I don't think it ever will be. It's like way too niche, but we have fun. (01:25:05): I would happily do it with my friends if no one was listening and then it's like, that's kind of wild that a bunch of people that we actually do care about find the pieces that are interesting. And it actually is helpful from a business perspective because you bullshit about something and then some entrepreneur shows up and is like, "Hey, by the way, here's a better idea." You're like, "That's great."
turns.zh: 所以关键是，我觉得人们……它在某种程度上是个有点怪的播客，因为老实说，我觉得我们谁都不怎么过滤，它差不多就像每周和朋友们聊一小时——而那正是我想做的。我爱 Morin 家。我们住得没那么近。（01:23:54）：所以把那段时间留出来、然后剪一剪、相当原始地发到网上，还挺好玩的。关于它，好笑的事在这儿。它对我们目的的满足，远超我实际预期——也就是我们享受做它，那是最重要的部分。就算没人在听，我们也会做。而诡异地，我们很多朋友、以及我们在意的那群行业里的人，似乎会捡起他们喜欢的那几段、然后跟我们聊。（01:24:19）：所以它就像个很棒的对话开场白。所以它有点诡异。它不是个巨大的播客。它够大，但我其实觉得，关于它最让我意外的是：尽管我们真没什么增长策略、也不想把它搞爆、而且我们也不拿钱，它却诡异地有用——这是我会下的判语。就连它像……我不知道。（01:24:41）：我不确定你是不是也有这体验，而且我觉得你的播客大概比我们大得多，但它诡异地被我们在意的那群人收听、并且有用，而且好玩——尽管它还不像……我不知道，它还没到全力以赴什么的。我觉得它永远也不会。它太垂直了，但我们玩得开心。（01:25:05）：如果没人在听，我也会乐呵呵地和朋友们做它；然后就像，我们真正在意的那么一伙人，会找到那些有意思的片段——这有点狂野。而且从生意角度，它其实有用，因为你瞎聊点什么，然后某个创业者冒出来像：『嘿，顺便说，这有个更好的点子。』你就想：『那太棒了。』

I appreciate you having me on. It's always fun to see you. It's been too long and I don't know. Come hang out in the pool house sometime.

turns.en: Okay. I love this. This is an excuse to hang out. Sam, thank you so much for being here.
